title: Chapter 9
paragraphs: "Oblonsky's carriage!" the porter shouted in a gruff bass. The carriage pulled up and both men got in. It was only for the first few moments, as the carriage rolled out of the clubhouse gates, that Levin was still under the spell of the club—the air of rest, comfort, and impeccable form. But as soon as the carriage hit the street and he felt it jolt over the uneven road, heard the angry shout of a sledge driver coming the other way, and saw in the half-light the red blind of a tavern and the shop windows, the spell broke, and he began to turn over what he'd done and wonder whether he was right to be going to see Anna. What would Kitty say? But Stepan Arkadyevitch gave him no time to think, and as if reading his doubts, swept them aside.

"How glad I am," he said, "that you're going to know her! Dolly has wanted this for ages. And Lvov has been to see her, and goes often. She may be my sister," Stepan Arkadyevitch went on, "but I'll say it anyway—she's a remarkable woman. You'll see. Her situation is very painful, especially right now."
"Why especially now?"

"We're negotiating with her husband about a divorce. He's agreed; but there are complications about the boy, and the whole thing—which should have been settled long ago—has dragged on for three months now. As soon as the divorce is through, she'll marry Vronsky. How stupid these old ceremonies are, that nobody believes in and that only get in the way of people being happy!" Stepan Arkadyevitch put in. "Anyway, once it's done, their position will be as regular as mine, as yours."
"What's the holdup?" said Levin.

"Oh, it's a long and tiresome story! The whole business is in such an awkward place here. The point is, she's been in Moscow for three months, where everyone knows her, waiting for the divorce; she goes out nowhere, sees no woman except Dolly, because, you understand, she doesn't want people coming as a favor. Even that fool Princess Varvara has dropped her, considering it a breach of propriety. Now, you see, any other woman in her position wouldn't have managed. But you'll see how she has arranged her life—how calm, how dignified she is. Left, in the crescent across from the church!" Stepan Arkadyevitch shouted, leaning out of the window. "Phew! it's hot!" he said, despite the twelve degrees of frost, throwing his already-open overcoat even wider.
"But she has a daughter—surely she's busy looking after her?" said Levin.

"I think you picture every woman simply as a female, _une couveuse_," said Stepan Arkadyevitch. "If she's occupied, it has to be with children. No—she's bringing her up well, I believe, but you don't hear about it. She's busy, first of all, with what she's writing. I see you're smiling skeptically, but you shouldn't be. She's writing a children's book, and never says a word about it to anyone, but she read it to me and I gave the manuscript to Vorkuev ... you know the publisher ... he's an author himself, I think. He understands these things, and he says it's a remarkable piece of work. But are you imagining she's some authoress?—not a bit of it. She's a woman with a heart, before anything else, but you'll see. Right now she has a little English girl living with her, and a whole family she's looking after."
"Oh, something philanthropic?"

"Why must you take everything in the worst sense? It's not philanthropy, it's from the heart. They—meaning Vronsky—had a trainer, an Englishman, first-rate at his job, but a drunk. He's completely lost to drink—delirium tremens—and his family was left destitute. She saw them, helped them, got more and more involved, and now the whole family is on her hands. And not as patronage, you know, throwing money at it; she's coaching the boys herself in Russian to prepare them for the high school, and she's taken the little girl in to live with her. But you'll see for yourself."
The carriage pulled into the courtyard, and Stepan Arkadyevitch rang loudly at the entrance, where several sledges were standing.

And without bothering to ask the servant who opened the door whether the lady was at home, Stepan Arkadyevitch walked straight into the hall. Levin followed, more and more uncertain whether he was doing the right thing or the wrong one.

Glancing at himself in the glass, Levin noticed his face was flushed, but he was sure he wasn't drunk, and he followed Stepan Arkadyevitch up the carpeted stairs. At the top, Stepan Arkadyevitch asked the footman, who bowed to him like a close friend, who was with Anna Arkadyevna, and got the answer: M. Vorkuev.
"Where are they?"
"In the study."

Walking through the dining-room—a smallish room with dark, paneled walls—Stepan Arkadyevitch and Levin crossed the soft carpet to the half-dark study, lit only by a single lamp with a big dark shade. Another lamp with a reflector was mounted on the wall, lighting up a large full-length portrait of a woman that Levin couldn't help looking at. It was the portrait of Anna, painted in Italy by Mihailov. While Stepan Arkadyevitch went past the _treillage_, and the male voice that had been speaking fell silent, Levin stood gazing at the portrait, which seemed to step out of its frame in the bright light thrown on it, and he could not pull himself away. He literally forgot where he was, and didn't even hear what was being said—he could not take his eyes off the marvelous portrait. It was not a picture but a living, beautiful woman, with dark curling hair, with bare arms and shoulders, with a thoughtful smile on lips covered with soft down; triumphantly and gently she looked at him with eyes that left him at a loss. She wasn't living only because she was more beautiful than any living woman can be.

"I'm delighted!" he heard a voice suddenly say close to him—clearly addressed to him, the voice of the very woman he had just been admiring in the portrait. Anna had come out from behind the _treillage_ to greet him, and in the dim light of the study Levin saw the very woman of the portrait, in a dark-blue shot dress, not in the same pose or with the same expression, but with the same beauty the artist had caught. She was less dazzling in real life, but on the other hand there was something fresh and alluring in the living woman that was not in the portrait.

title: Chapter 10
paragraphs: She had stood up to meet him, not hiding her pleasure at seeing him; and in the quiet, easy way she held out her small strong hand, introduced him to Vorkuev, and pointed to a red-haired, pretty little girl sitting at her work, calling her her pupil, Levin recognized and liked the manner of a woman of the great world—always composed and natural.

"I'm delighted, delighted," she said again, and in her voice these ordinary words took on a special weight for Levin. "I've known you and liked you for a long time, both through your friendship with Stiva and for your wife's sake.... I knew her only briefly, but she struck me as an exquisite flower, simply a flower. And to think she'll soon be a mother!"

She spoke easily and unhurriedly, glancing now and then from Levin to her brother, and Levin felt that the impression he was making on her was a good one, and right away he felt at home with her—simple and at ease, as though he'd known her since childhood.

"Ivan Petrovitch and I settled in Alexey's study," she said in answer to Stepan Arkadyevitch's question about whether he could smoke, "so we could smoke"—and glancing at Levin, instead of asking whether he smoked, she pulled a tortoiseshell cigar-case closer and took a cigarette.
"How are you feeling today?" her brother asked.
"Oh, nothing. Nerves, as usual."
"It really is extraordinary, isn't it?" said Stepan Arkadyevitch, noticing that Levin was studying the picture.
"I've never seen a better portrait."
"And remarkably like her, isn't it?" Vorkuev said.

Levin looked from the portrait back to the original. A peculiar brightness lit up Anna's face when she felt his eyes on her. Levin flushed, and to cover his embarrassment was about to ask whether she had seen Darya Alexandrovna lately; but at that moment Anna spoke. "Ivan Petrovitch and I were just talking about Vashtchenkov's latest pictures. Have you seen them?"
"Yes, I have," Levin answered.
"Forgive me, I interrupted you ... you were saying?..."
Levin asked whether she had seen Dolly lately.
"She was here yesterday. She was very upset with the high school people on Grisha's account. The Latin teacher, apparently, had been unfair to him."
"Yes, I saw his pictures. I didn't care for them much," Levin said, going back to the topic she had raised.

Levin was no longer talking in the strictly businesslike way he'd been talking all morning. Every word in his conversation with her carried a special weight. And it was pleasant to talk to her; even more pleasant to listen.
Anna talked not just naturally and intelligently but intelligently and without insistence, attaching no weight to her own ideas and giving a great deal to whatever the other person said.
The conversation turned to the new movement in art, and to a French artist's new illustrations of the Bible. Vorkuev attacked the artist for a realism pushed to the point of coarseness.
Levin said the French had carried artifice further than anyone else, and that as a result they saw great merit in the return to realism. The act of not lying was, to them, poetry.
Nothing clever Levin had ever said had given him so much pleasure as this remark. Anna's face lit up at once, as she at once understood the thought. She laughed.

"I laugh," she said, "the way one laughs at a very accurate portrait. What you just said is perfectly true of French art now—painting, and literature too, in fact—Zola, Daudet. But maybe it's always like that: people first build their ideas of human nature out of made-up, conventional types, and then—once all the _combinaisons_ have been worked through—they get tired of those invented figures and start trying to invent more natural, more truthful ones."
"That's perfectly true," said Vorkuev.
"So you've been at the club?" she said to her brother.

"Yes, yes, this is a woman!" Levin thought, forgetting himself and staring fixedly at her lovely, mobile face, which at that moment was suddenly completely transformed. Levin didn't hear what she was talking about as she leaned over to her brother, but the change in her expression struck him. Her face—so handsome a moment before in its repose—suddenly took on a look of strange curiosity, anger, and pride. But it lasted only an instant. She lowered her eyelids, as though remembering something.
"Oh, well, but that's of no interest to anyone," she said, and turned to the English girl.
"Please order the tea in the drawing-room," she said in English.
The girl got up and went out.
"So how did she do on her exam?" Stepan Arkadyevitch asked.
"Splendidly! She's a very gifted child and a sweet character."
"It'll end with you loving her more than your own."
"That's a man speaking. In love there's no more or less. I love my daughter with one kind of love, and her with another."

"I was just telling Anna Arkadyevna," Vorkuev said, "that if she put even a hundredth of the energy she devotes to this English girl into the public question of educating Russian children, she would be doing great and useful work."

"Yes, but I can't help it; I just couldn't do it. Count Alexey Kirillovitch pressed me very hard" (as she said the words _Count Alexey Kirillovitch_ she glanced at Levin with an appealing shyness, and he answered without thinking with a respectful, reassuring look); "he pressed me to take up the school in the village. I went there several times. The children were lovely, but I couldn't feel drawn to the work. You talk about energy. Energy rests on love; and love comes how it will—you can't force it. I took to this child—I couldn't say myself why."

And she glanced at Levin again. And her smile and her look—both told him that her words were really meant for him alone, that she valued his opinion, and at the same time was sure in advance that he understood her.

"I understand that completely," Levin said. "It's impossible to give your heart to a school, or to that sort of institution in general, and I think that's exactly why philanthropic projects always produce such poor results."
She was silent for a moment, then smiled.

"Yes, yes," she agreed; "I never could. _Je n'ai pas le cœur assez_ large to love a whole asylum full of horrid little girls. _Cela ne m'a jamais réussi._ There are so many women who have made themselves _une position sociale_ that way. And now more than ever," she said with a sad, confiding expression, supposedly speaking to her brother but plainly meaning the words for Levin alone, "now, when I have such a need for some occupation, I can't." And suddenly frowning (Levin saw that she was frowning at herself for talking about herself), she changed the subject. "I know about you," she said to Levin; "that you're not a public-spirited citizen, and I have defended you as best I could."
"How have you defended me?"
"Oh, depending on the attacks made against you. But won't you have some tea?" She rose and picked up a book bound in morocco.
"Let me have it, Anna Arkadyevna," said Vorkuev, pointing at the book. "It's well worth picking up."
"Oh no, it's all so rough."
"I told him about it," Stepan Arkadyevitch said to his sister, nodding toward Levin.

"You shouldn't have. My writing is like those little baskets and carved pieces that Liza Mertsalova used to sell me from the prisons. She was in charge of the prison department in that society," she explained, turning to Levin; "and they were miracles of patience, the work of those poor wretches."

And Levin saw a new trait in this woman who attracted him so extraordinarily. Besides wit, grace, and beauty, she had truth. She had no wish to hide from him the bitterness of her position. As she said this she sighed, and her face suddenly took on a hard expression, as if it had turned to stone. With that expression on her face she was more beautiful than ever; but the expression was new—nothing like the look, glowing with happiness and giving off happiness, that the painter had caught in her portrait. Levin glanced more than once at the portrait and at her figure as, taking her brother's arm, she walked with him to the tall doors, and he felt a tenderness and pity for her that surprised him.

She asked Levin and Vorkuev to go through to the drawing-room while she stayed behind to say a few words to her brother. "About her divorce, about Vronsky, about what he's doing at the club, about me?" Levin wondered. And he was so caught up in the question of what she was saying to Stepan Arkadyevitch that he barely heard Vorkuev's account of the qualities of the children's story Anna Arkadyevna had written.

At tea the same pleasant talk, full of interesting things, went on. There wasn't a single moment when you had to hunt for something to say; on the contrary, you felt you barely had time to say what you wanted to and were eagerly holding back to hear what the others would say. And everything that was said—not only by her, but by Vorkuev and Stepan Arkadyevitch—all of it, it seemed to Levin, took on a special meaning from her appreciation and her judgment. While he followed this interesting conversation, Levin kept admiring her—her beauty, her intelligence, her education, and at the same time her directness and the genuine depth of her feeling. He listened and talked, and the whole time he was thinking about her inner life, trying to guess at her feelings. And though he had judged her so harshly until now, by some strange chain of reasoning he was now justifying her and feeling sorry for her, and worrying that Vronsky did not fully understand her. At eleven o'clock, when Stepan Arkadyevitch got up to leave (Vorkuev had gone earlier), it seemed to Levin he had only just arrived. Reluctantly, Levin stood up too.
"Good-bye," she said, holding his hand and looking into his face with a winning expression. "I am very glad _que la glace est rompue._"
She let go of his hand and half closed her eyes.

"Tell your wife I love her as before, and that if she can't pardon me my position, then my wish for her is that she never has to pardon it. To pardon it, one has to have gone through what I have gone through, and may God spare her that."
"Of course, yes, I'll tell her...." Levin said, blushing.

title: Chapter 11
paragraphs: "What a marvelous, sweet, unhappy woman!" he was thinking, as he stepped out into the frosty air with Stepan Arkadyevitch.
"Well, didn't I tell you?" said Stepan Arkadyevitch, seeing that Levin had been entirely won over.
"Yes," Levin said dreamily, "an extraordinary woman! It's not her cleverness—it's that wonderful depth of feeling. I feel terribly sorry for her!"

"Now, please God, the whole thing will soon be sorted out. Well, well, don't be too hard on people from now on," said Stepan Arkadyevitch, opening the carriage door. "Good night; we don't go the same way."

Still thinking of Anna—of everything, even the simplest line in their conversation, recalling the smallest changes in her expression, entering more and more into her position, feeling sorry for her—Levin got home.

At home, Kouzma told Levin that Katerina Alexandrovna was perfectly well, that her sisters had not long since left, and handed him two letters. Levin read them right there in the hall, so he wouldn't forget them later. One was from Sokolov, his bailiff. Sokolov wrote that the corn could not be sold, that the best price on offer was five and a half roubles, and that nothing more was to be had. The other letter was from his sister. She scolded him because her business was still unsettled.

"Well, we'll sell at five and a half if we can't get more," Levin decided the first question—a question that had always seemed so weighty before—with an extraordinary ease right there on the spot. "Amazing how all your time is taken up here," he thought, considering the second letter. He blamed himself for not having done what his sister had asked him to do. "Today again I didn't go to the court—but today I really didn't have time." And resolving that he wouldn't fail to do it the next day, he went upstairs to his wife. As he went in, Levin ran quickly back through the day. All the events of it were conversations—conversations he'd heard and taken part in. All those conversations were about subjects he would never have brought up if he'd been at home alone, but here they had been very interesting. And all the conversations had been all right, except in two places, where something wasn't quite right. One was what he had said about the carp; the other was something not "quite the thing" in the tender sympathy he was feeling for Anna.

Levin found his wife low-spirited and dull. The dinner of the three sisters had gone off very well, but then they had waited and waited for him, all of them had grown bored, the sisters had left, and she had been alone.

"Well, and what have you been doing?" she asked, looking straight into his eyes, which shone with a rather suspicious brightness. But so she wouldn't keep him from telling her everything, she hid her close watchfulness and listened with an approving smile to his account of how he had spent the evening.

"Well, I'm very glad I ran into Vronsky. I felt completely at ease and natural with him. You understand, I'll try not to see him, but I'm glad that this awkwardness is over with," he said, and remembering that as his way of trying not to see Vronsky he had gone straight from the club to call on Anna, he blushed. "We talk about peasants drinking; I'm not sure who drinks more, the peasants or our own class. The peasants do on holidays, but...."
But Kitty had no interest at all in discussing peasant drinking habits. She had seen him blush, and she wanted to know why.
"Well, and then where did you go?"
"Stiva pressed me hard to go and see Anna Arkadyevna."
And as he said it, Levin blushed even more deeply, and his doubts about whether he'd done right in going to see Anna were settled once and for all. He knew now that he should not have done it.
Kitty's eyes opened in a strange way and flashed at Anna's name, but with an effort she controlled herself, hid her feeling, and misled him.
"Oh!" was all she said.
"I'm sure you won't be angry with me for going. Stiva begged me to, and Dolly wanted it," Levin went on.
"Oh, no!" she said, but he saw in her eyes a tightness that boded no good.
"She's a very sweet, very, very unhappy, good woman," he said, telling her about Anna, what she was doing, and the message Anna had asked him to pass on.
"Yes, of course, she's much to be pitied," Kitty said, when he was done. "Whom was your letter from?"
He told her, and trusting her calm tone, he went off to change his coat.
When he came back, he found Kitty in the same armchair. As he walked up to her, she looked up at him and burst into sobs.
"What? what is it?" he asked, knowing perfectly well what.

"You're in love with that hateful woman; she has bewitched you! I saw it in your eyes. Yes, yes! Where can this lead? You were drinking at the club, drinking and gambling, and then you went ... to her of all people! No, we have to leave.... I'll go tomorrow."

It was a long while before Levin could calm his wife. In the end he managed it only by admitting that a feeling of pity, combined with the wine he had drunk, had got the better of him, that he had fallen under Anna's clever influence, and that he would avoid her. The one thing he confessed more honestly was that living so long in Moscow—a life of nothing but talk, eating and drinking—he was going to seed. They talked until three in the morning. Only at three were they reconciled enough to be able to sleep.

title: Chapter 12
paragraphs: After saying goodbye to her guests, Anna did not sit down but started pacing up and down the room. She had, without quite meaning to, spent the whole evening doing her utmost to spark a feeling of love in Levin—as lately she had been doing with all young men—and she knew she had managed it, as far as one can in a single evening with a married and conscientious man. She did like him a great deal, and despite the striking difference between Vronsky and Levin from a man's point of view, as a woman she could see something they had in common, something that had made it possible for Kitty to love both of them. Yet as soon as he was out of the room, she stopped thinking about him.

One thought, and only one, kept chasing her in different forms, and would not leave her alone. "If I can have so much effect on others—on this man, who loves his home and his wife—why is _he_ so cold to me?... not cold, exactly, he loves me, I know that! But something new is pulling us apart now. Why wasn't he here all evening? He sent word through Stiva that he couldn't leave Yashvin and had to watch over his play. Is Yashvin a child? But suppose it's true. He never lies. But if it's true, there's something else in it. He's glad of a chance to show me he has other duties; I know that, I accept that. But why does he have to prove it to me? He wants to show me that his love for me isn't going to interfere with his freedom. But I don't need proofs—I need love. He ought to understand how bitter this life is for me here in Moscow. Is this a life? I'm not living, I'm waiting for something that keeps being put off and put off. Still no answer! And Stiva says he can't go to Alexey Alexandrovitch. And I can't write again. I can do nothing, start nothing, change nothing. I hold myself in, I wait, inventing amusements—the English family, my writing, reading—but it's all a sham, it's all the same as morphine. He ought to feel for me," she said, feeling tears of self-pity rising in her eyes.

She heard Vronsky's abrupt ring and quickly dried her tears—not only dried them, but sat down by a lamp and opened a book, putting on an air of composure. She wanted him to see that she was annoyed he hadn't come home when he promised—just annoyed, and on no account to let him see her distress, least of all her self-pity. She might pity herself, but he must not pity her. She didn't want a quarrel, she blamed him for wanting one, but without realizing it, she settled into a stance of attack.
"Well, you weren't bored?" he said, eagerly and good-humoredly, as he came up to her. "What a terrible passion it is—gambling!"
"No, I wasn't bored; I learned long ago how not to be bored. Stiva was here, and Levin."
"Yes, they meant to come and see you. Well, how did you like Levin?" he said, sitting down beside her.
"Very much. They haven't long been gone. What was Yashvin doing?"
"He was winning—seventeen thousand. I got him to leave. He'd actually started for home, but then he turned around, and now he's losing."

"Then why did you stay?" she asked, suddenly lifting her eyes to him. The expression on her face was cold and ungracious. "You told Stiva you were staying to get Yashvin away. And you left him there."
The same expression of cold readiness for a fight came over his face too.

"In the first place, I didn't ask him to bring you any message; and second, I never lie. But what matters most is that I wanted to stay, and I stayed," he said, frowning. "Anna, what is this for, why are you doing this?" he said after a moment's silence, leaning toward her and opening his hand, hoping she would put hers in it.
She was glad of this appeal for tenderness. But some strange, evil force would not let her give in to her feelings, as though the rules of war would not let her surrender.

"Of course you wanted to stay, and you stayed. You do whatever you want. But why are you telling me that? What for?" she said, growing more and more agitated. "Is anyone disputing your rights? But you want to be right, and by all means be right."
His hand closed, he turned away, and his face took on an even more stubborn expression.

"For you it's a matter of stubbornness," she said, watching him intently and suddenly hitting on the right word for the look that irritated her, "simple stubbornness. For you it's a question of whether you keep the upper hand of me, and for me...." Again she felt sorry for herself, and almost burst into tears. "If you knew what this is for me! When I feel, as I do now, that you are hostile—yes, hostile to me—if you knew what that means for me! If you knew how I feel on the brink of disaster at this very moment, how afraid I am of myself!" And she turned away, hiding her sobs.

"But what are you talking about?" he said, horrified at her look of despair, and bending over her again, he took her hand and kissed it. "What is it for? Am I looking for amusements outside our home? Don't I avoid the company of women?"
"Well, yes! If only that were all!" she said.

"Come, tell me what I ought to do to give you peace of mind? I'm ready to do anything to make you happy," he said, moved by her look of despair; "what wouldn't I do to spare you any distress, as now, Anna!" he said.

"It's nothing, nothing!" she said. "I don't know myself whether it's the loneliness, my nerves.... Come, let's not talk about it. What about the race? You haven't told me!" she asked, trying to hide her triumph at the victory which, in the end, had been hers.

He asked for supper and began telling her about the races; but in his voice, in his eyes, which grew colder and colder, she saw he did not forgive her her victory, that the stubborn streak she had been fighting had reasserted itself in him. He was cooler with her than before, as though he regretted having given in. And she, remembering the words that had won her the victory—"how I feel on the brink of disaster, how afraid I am of myself"—saw that this was a dangerous weapon, and that she could not use it a second time. And she felt that alongside the love that bound them together, there had grown up some evil spirit of conflict between them, one she could not drive out of his heart, and still less out of her own.

title: Chapter 13
paragraphs: There are no circumstances a man cannot get used to, especially when he sees everyone around him living the same way. Three months earlier, Levin could not have believed that he would be able to fall calmly asleep in the state he was in that day—living an aimless, irrational life, spending beyond his means, after drinking to excess (he couldn't call what had happened at the club anything else), forming an inappropriately friendly relationship with a man his wife had once been in love with, and paying a still more inappropriate visit to a woman who could only be called a lost woman, after being charmed by that woman and upsetting his wife—he could still drop quietly off to sleep. But under the effect of exhaustion, a sleepless night, and the wine he had drunk, his sleep was sound and untroubled.
At five o'clock the creak of a door opening woke him. He jumped up and looked around. Kitty was not in bed beside him. But there was a light moving behind the screen, and he could hear her footsteps.
"What is it?... what is it?" he said, half-asleep. "Kitty! What is it?"
"Nothing," she said, coming out from behind the screen with a candle in her hand. "I wasn't feeling well," she said, with a particularly sweet and knowing smile.
"What? has it started?" he said in alarm. "We need to send...." and he hurriedly reached for his clothes.
"No, no," she said, smiling and holding his hand. "It's almost certainly nothing. I was just a bit unwell. It's over now."

And climbing back into bed, she blew out the candle, lay down, and was still. Though her stillness struck him as suspicious—as if she were holding her breath—and even more suspicious was the look of peculiar tenderness and excitement she had worn coming out from behind the screen as she said "nothing," he was so sleepy that he dropped off at once. Only later did he remember the stillness of her breathing, and understand everything that must have been happening in her sweet, precious heart while she lay beside him, not moving, awaiting the greatest event in a woman's life. At seven o'clock he was woken by her hand on his shoulder and a gentle whisper. She seemed to be torn between regret at waking him and the wish to talk to him.
"Kostya, don't be frightened. It's all right. But I think.... We ought to send for Lizaveta Petrovna."
The candle was lit again. She was sitting up in bed, holding some knitting she had been working on these last few days.
"Please, don't be frightened, it's all right. I'm not the least bit afraid," she said, seeing his terrified face, and she pressed his hand to her breast, then to her lips.

He jumped up quickly, still barely awake, and kept his eyes fixed on her as he pulled on his dressing gown; then he stopped, still looking at her. He had to go, but he could not tear himself away from her eyes. He thought he loved her face, knew her expression, her eyes, but he had never seen her like this. How hateful and awful he seemed to himself, thinking of the distress he had caused her the day before. Her flushed face, framed by soft curling hair under her night cap, was radiant with joy and courage.

Though there was so little that was complicated or artificial in Kitty's nature in general, Levin was struck by what was now showing through, when suddenly all the layers fell away and the very core of her soul shone out of her eyes. And in this simplicity, this nakedness of her soul, she—the very woman he loved in her—was clearer than ever. She looked at him, smiling; but all at once her brows twitched, she lifted her head, and walking quickly up to him, gripped his hand and pressed close to him, breathing her hot breath against him. She was in pain and was, as it were, complaining to him of her suffering. And for the first moment, out of habit, it seemed to him that he was to blame. But in her eyes there was a tenderness that told him she was nowhere near reproaching him, that she loved him for her suffering. "If not I, who is to blame for it?" he thought without meaning to, looking for someone to hold responsible for this pain so that he could punish them; but there was no one. She was suffering, complaining, and triumphing in her suffering, and rejoicing in it, and loving it. He saw that something sublime was being accomplished in her soul, but what? He could not figure it out. It was beyond him.
"I've sent for Mamma. You go quickly and bring Lizaveta Petrovna ... Kostya!... Nothing, it's passed."
She stepped away from him and rang the bell.
"Right, go now; Pasha's coming. I'm all right."
And Levin saw with astonishment that she had picked up the knitting she had brought in during the night and started working at it again.
As Levin was going out one door, he heard the maidservant come in at the other. He paused at the door and heard Kitty giving the maid precise instructions and starting to help her move the bed.

He dressed, and while they were harnessing his horses—since no cab for hire was in sight yet—he ran back up to the bedroom, not on tiptoe, it seemed to him, but on wings. Two maidservants were carefully moving something in the room.
Kitty was walking about, knitting quickly and giving directions.
"I'm going for the doctor. They've sent for Lizaveta Petrovna, but I'll go on there too. Isn't there anything wanted? Should I stop by Dolly's?"
She looked at him, plainly not hearing what he was saying.
"Yes, yes. Do go," she said quickly, frowning and waving him off with her hand.
He had just stepped into the drawing-room when suddenly a plaintive moan sounded from the bedroom, instantly cut short. He stood still, and for a long while could not take it in.
"Yes, that's her," he said to himself, and clutching his head, he ran downstairs.

"Lord have mercy on us! pardon us! help us!" he repeated, the words coming for some reason suddenly to his lips. And he, an unbeliever, repeated these words not just with his lips. In that instant he knew that all his doubts—even the impossibility of believing through reason, which he was aware of in himself—did not in the least keep him from turning to God. All of that now floated out of his soul like dust. Whom was he to turn to if not to Him in whose hands he felt himself, his soul, and his love?

The horse wasn't ready yet, but feeling an unusual concentration of his physical strength and his mind on what he had to do, he set out on foot without waiting for it, and told Kouzma to catch up with him.

At the corner he met a night cabman driving fast. In the small sledge, wrapped in a velvet cloak, sat Lizaveta Petrovna, a kerchief tied round her head. "Thank God! thank God!" he said, overjoyed to recognize her small, fair face, which wore a peculiarly serious, almost stern expression. Telling the driver not to stop, he ran along beside her.
"Two hours, then? No more?" she asked. "You ought to let Pyotr Dmitrievitch know, but don't hurry him. And get some opium at the chemist's."

"So you think it may go well? Lord have mercy on us and help us!" Levin said, seeing his own horse driving out through the gate. Jumping into the sledge beside Kouzma, he told him to drive to the doctor's.

title: Chapter 14
paragraphs: The doctor was not yet up. The footman said he had been up late and had given orders not to be woken, but would be up soon. The footman was busy cleaning the lamp-chimneys and seemed entirely absorbed in them. His concentration on his lamps, and his indifference to whatever Levin was going through, stunned Levin at first; but as soon as he thought it over he understood that no one knew or was obliged to know what he was feeling, and that it was therefore all the more important to act calmly, sensibly, and with resolve in order to break through this wall of indifference and get what he had come for.
"Don't rush, don't let anything slip," Levin told himself, feeling a steadily rising surge of physical energy and focus on everything he had to do.

Once he had confirmed that the doctor was not getting up, Levin ran through several plans and settled on this one: Kouzma would go fetch another doctor while he himself went to the chemist's for opium; and if, when he returned, the doctor had still not stirred, he would either tip the footman or — failing that — force his way in and wake the doctor by any means necessary.

At the chemist's, the lanky assistant was sealing up a packet of powders for a waiting coachman, and he refused Levin the opium with the same flat indifference the doctor's footman had shown for his lamps. Trying not to flare up or fall apart, Levin named the doctor and the midwife, explained what the opium was for, and tried to talk him round. The assistant called something in German through a partition, got an affirmative answer from the back, took out a bottle and a funnel, and deliberately poured the opium from a larger bottle into a small one, stuck on a label, and sealed it — over Levin's protests — and was about to wrap it as well. That was more than Levin could take; he snatched the bottle out of the man's hands and ran for the big glass doors. The doctor still was not up, and the footman, now busy laying out rugs, refused to wake him. Levin took out a ten-rouble note deliberately, and forcing himself to speak slowly — though wasting no time — handed it over and explained that Pyotr Dmitrievitch (what a great and weighty personage this Pyotr Dmitrievitch now seemed to Levin, when only yesterday the man had barely registered!) had promised to come at any hour, that he would certainly not be angry, and that he had to be woken at once.
The footman agreed, went upstairs, and showed Levin into the waiting room.
Through the door Levin could hear the doctor coughing, moving about, washing, saying something. Three minutes went by; to Levin it felt like more than an hour. He could not wait any longer.
"Pyotr Dmitrievitch, Pyotr Dmitrievitch!" he said pleadingly at the open door. "For God's sake, forgive me — see me as you are. It's been going on more than two hours already."
"One minute, one minute!" came the answer, and to Levin's astonishment he could hear that the doctor was smiling as he said it.
"Just for a second."
"One minute."
Two more minutes passed while the doctor pulled on his boots, and two more while he put on his coat and combed his hair.

"Pyotr Dmitrievitch!" Levin was beginning again in a despairing voice, just as the doctor walked in, dressed and ready. "These people have no conscience," Levin thought. "Combing his hair while we're dying!"
"Good morning!" said the doctor, shaking his hand and, with his calmness, almost seeming to tease him. "There's no rush. Well now?"
Doing his best to be precise, Levin began telling him every unnecessary detail about his wife's condition, breaking off again and again to beg the doctor to come with him at once.

"There's really no need to rush. You don't understand, you see. I'm sure I'm not needed yet — but I've promised, so if you like, I'll come. There's no hurry. Please, sit down. Won't you have some coffee?"
Levin stared at him as if asking whether he was being mocked; but the doctor had no thought of mocking him.

"I know, I know," said the doctor, smiling. "I'm a married man myself, and at moments like this we husbands deserve a great deal of sympathy. I have a patient whose husband always takes refuge in the stables when the time comes."
"But what do you think, Pyotr Dmitrievitch? Do you think it will go all right?"
"Everything points to a good outcome."
"So you'll come at once?" Levin said, glaring at the servant who was bringing in the coffee.
"In an hour."
"Oh, for God's sake!"
"Well — let me drink my coffee, at least."
The doctor started on his coffee. Both were silent.
"The Turks really are getting a beating, though. Did you see yesterday's telegrams?" the doctor said, chewing on a roll.
"No, I can't stand this!" Levin said, jumping up. "So you'll be with us in a quarter of an hour?"
"Half an hour."
"On your honor?"

When Levin got home, he pulled up at the same moment as the princess, and they went up to the bedroom door together. The princess had tears in her eyes and her hands were shaking. The moment she saw Levin she threw her arms around him and burst into tears.
"Well, my dear Lizaveta Petrovna?" she asked, gripping the hand of the midwife, who came out to meet them with a glowing, anxious face.
"She's coming along well," the midwife said. "Persuade her to lie down. She'll be more comfortable that way."

From the moment he had woken up and grasped what was happening, Levin had set his mind to bear the day resolutely, without thinking ahead or trying to anticipate anything, simply so as not to upset his wife — and instead to soothe her and keep her courage up. Without letting himself think about what was coming, or how it would end, and going by what he'd been told about how long such ordeals usually lasted, Levin had braced himself, in his imagination, to hold steady and keep a tight rein on himself for five hours; and it had seemed to him he could manage that. But when he came back from the doctor's and saw her suffering again, he began saying, more and more often, "Lord, have mercy on us, and help us!" He kept sighing, throwing his head back, and beginning to fear he couldn't bear it — that he was going to burst into tears or run from the room. That was the agony of it for him. And only one hour had passed.

But after that hour came another, and another, and another — the full five hours he had set as the outer limit of his endurance — and the situation was unchanged; and he was still bearing it, because there was nothing to do but bear it, every moment certain he had reached the very end of what he could take, and that his heart would crack from sympathy and pain.
And still the minutes and the hours kept going by, more hours after that, and his misery and dread only grew sharper and sharper.

All the ordinary conditions of life — the ones that ordinarily frame how you make sense of anything — had stopped existing for Levin. He lost all sense of time. Minutes — those minutes when she called for him and he held her damp hand that would clamp down on his with shocking force and then shove it away — felt like hours, and hours felt like minutes. He was startled when Lizaveta Petrovna asked him to light a candle behind a screen and he realized it was five in the afternoon. If she had told him it was ten in the morning, he would not have been any more surprised. Where he had been all this while, he knew about as much as he knew about the passage of time. He saw Kitty's swollen face — at moments bewildered and in agony, at moments smiling and trying to reassure him. He saw the old princess too, flushed and overwrought, her grey curls in disarray, forcing herself to swallow her tears, biting her lips; he saw Dolly, and the doctor smoking fat cigarettes, and Lizaveta Petrovna with her firm, resolute, reassuring face, and the old prince pacing the hall with a frown. But why they kept coming in and going out, and where they were, he did not know. The princess was with the doctor in the bedroom; then in the study, where a table set for dinner had appeared from nowhere; then she was gone and Dolly was there instead. Then Levin remembered he had been sent somewhere. Once he was sent to move a table and sofa. He had done it eagerly, thinking it had to be done for her sake, and only later realized it was his own bed he had been getting ready. Then he was sent to the study to ask the doctor something. The doctor had answered, and then started in on the irregularities in the municipal council. Then he had been sent to the bedroom to help the old princess move the icon in its silver and gold setting, and with the princess's old lady's maid he had climbed up on a shelf to reach it and broken the little lamp, and the old servant had tried to comfort him about the lamp and about his wife, and he had carried the icon and set it at Kitty's head, carefully tucking it in behind the pillow. But where and when and why any of this had happened he could not have said. He did not understand why the old princess took his hand and looked at him with pity and begged him not to torment himself, and why Dolly coaxed him into eating something and led him out of the room, and why even the doctor looked at him gravely and with sympathy and offered him a drop of something.

All he knew, all he felt, was that what was happening was what had happened nearly a year before in the country town's hotel, at the deathbed of his brother Nikolay. But that had been grief — this was joy. And yet that grief and this joy stood equally outside all the ordinary terms of life; they were a kind of opening in ordinary life through which one caught a glimpse of something sublime. And in the contemplation of that sublime something, the soul was lifted to heights it had never imagined, while reason limped behind, unable to keep up.

"Lord, have mercy on us, and help us!" he kept repeating to himself, feeling — despite his long, and as it had seemed complete, drift away from religion — that he was turning to God just as trustingly and simply as he had as a child and a very young man.

All through this he was in two distinct states of soul. One was when he was away from her — with the doctor, who kept smoking one fat cigarette after another and stubbing them out on the edge of an overflowing ashtray; with Dolly; and with the old prince, where the talk was about dinner, about politics, about Marya Petrovna's illness, and where Levin would suddenly forget for a minute what was going on and feel as though he had just woken from sleep. The other was at her bedside, where his heart felt as if it were breaking and somehow still did not break from the sympathy of suffering with her, and where he prayed to God without stopping. And every time some scream from the bedroom yanked him out of a moment of forgetting, he fell back into the same strange terror that had hit him in the first minute. Every time he heard a cry, he leapt up, ran to defend himself, remembered on the way that he wasn't to blame, and longed to defend her, to help her. But once he looked at her again, he saw again that help was impossible, and he was filled with terror and prayed, "Lord, have mercy on us, and help us!" And as time went on, both states grew more intense; the calmer he became away from her, completely forgetting her, the more unbearable her suffering and his helplessness in the face of it became. He would jump up, want to bolt — and run to her instead.

Sometimes, when she called for him again and again, he blamed her; but then, seeing her patient, smiling face and hearing the words, "I'm wearing you out," he turned and blamed God; and then, thinking of God, he immediately began begging God to forgive him and have mercy.

title: Chapter 15
paragraphs: He could not tell whether it was late or early. The candles had all burned down. Dolly had just been in the study and had suggested that the doctor lie down. Levin sat listening to the doctor's stories about a quack mesmerist and staring at the ash on his cigarette. There had been a stretch of calm, and he had sunk into a kind of blankness. He had completely forgotten what was going on right now. He was hearing the doctor's chatter and following it. Suddenly an unearthly shriek came through. The shriek was so awful that Levin did not even jump up; he held his breath and looked at the doctor with terrified questioning eyes. The doctor cocked his head, listened, and gave an approving smile. Everything was so extraordinary that nothing struck Levin as strange anymore. "I suppose that's how it has to be," he thought, and stayed where he was. Whose scream was that? He jumped up, ran on tiptoe to the bedroom, edged around Lizaveta Petrovna and the princess, and took his place at Kitty's pillow. The scream had stopped, but something had changed. What it was he didn't see and didn't take in, and he had no wish to see or take it in. But he could read it on Lizaveta Petrovna's face. Her face was stern and pale, still as resolute as ever, though her jaw was twitching and her eyes were fixed on Kitty. Kitty's swollen, anguished face, a lock of hair stuck to her damp forehead, was turned to him, searching for his eyes. Her raised hands reached for his. Clutching his cold hands in her hot, wet ones, she began pressing them to her face.
"Don't go, don't go! I'm not afraid, I'm not afraid!" she said quickly. "Mamma, take my earrings. They're bothering me. You're not afraid? Quick, quick, Lizaveta Petrovna...."
She spoke fast, very fast, and tried to smile. But suddenly her face contorted and she pushed him away.
"Oh, this is horrible! I'm dying, I'm dying! Go away!" she shrieked, and again that unearthly scream tore out of her.
Levin clutched his head and ran out of the room.
"It's nothing, it's nothing, it's all fine," Dolly called after him.

But they could say what they liked — he knew now that it was over. He stood in the next room, his head leaning against the doorpost, and listened to shrieks and howls of a kind he had never heard before, and he knew that what had been Kitty was making these sounds. He had long since stopped wanting the child. By now he hated this child. He did not even want her to survive anymore. All he wanted was for this terrible agony to end.
"Doctor! What is it? What is it? My God!" he said, grabbing at the doctor's hand as he came up.
"It's the end," the doctor said. And the doctor's face was so grave as he said it that Levin took _the end_ to mean her death.

Out of his mind, he ran into the bedroom. The first thing he saw was Lizaveta Petrovna's face. It was even more frowning and stern. Kitty's face he could not even recognize. In its place was something fearful in its strained distortion and in the sounds coming out of it. He sank down with his head on the wooden frame of the bed, feeling that his heart was bursting. The awful scream went on and on, and grew worse, and just when it seemed to have hit the absolute outer limit of horror, it stopped. Levin could not believe his ears, but there was no doubt: the scream had stopped, and he could hear a hushed bustle, hurried breathing, and her voice — gasping, alive, tender, blissful — saying softly, "It's over!"
He lifted his head. Her hands lay exhausted on the quilt; she looked extraordinarily lovely and serene; she looked at him in silence and tried to smile, and couldn't.

And suddenly, out of the mysterious and dreadful far-off world he had been living in for the last twenty-two hours, Levin felt himself thrown, in one instant, back into the ordinary everyday world — though now lit up with such a blaze of happiness that he could not bear it. The taut strings snapped; sobs and tears of joy he had never expected rose up with such force that his whole body shook, and for a long time they kept him from speaking.

Dropping to his knees by the bed, he held his wife's hand to his lips and kissed it, and her hand, with a weak movement of the fingers, answered his kiss. And meanwhile, there at the foot of the bed, in the practiced hands of Lizaveta Petrovna, like a flickering flame in a lamp, lay the life of a human being who had never existed before, and who would now, with the same right and the same significance to itself, live and create after its own kind.
"Alive! alive! And a boy too! Don't worry!" Levin heard Lizaveta Petrovna saying, as she slapped the baby's back with a shaking hand.
"Mamma, is it true?" came Kitty's voice.

The princess's sobs were all the answer she could give. And in the middle of the silence came, in unmistakable reply to the mother's question, a voice unlike any of the hushed voices in the room. It was the bold, clamorous, self-assertive squall of the new human being who had so inexplicably arrived.

If Levin had been told before this that Kitty was dead, and that he had died with her, and that their children were angels, and that God was standing in front of him, none of it would have surprised him. But now, coming back into the world of the actual, he had to make a real mental effort to take in that she was alive and well, and that this creature wailing so desperately was his son. Kitty was alive, her agony was over. And he was unspeakably happy. That he understood; he was completely happy in that. But the baby? Where from, why, who was he?... He could not get used to the idea. It felt like something extra, something superfluous, something he couldn't acclimatize himself to.

title: Chapter 16
paragraphs: At ten o'clock the old prince, Sergey Ivanovitch, and Stepan Arkadyevitch were sitting at Levin's. Once they had asked after Kitty, they had drifted into talk about other things. Levin listened, and without meaning to, as they talked, he kept going back over the past — over what his life had been right up to that morning — and thought of himself as he had been only yesterday up until that moment. It was as though a hundred years had passed since then. He felt himself lifted to heights no one could reach, from which he carefully lowered himself so as not to bruise the people he was talking with. He talked, and the whole time he was thinking of his wife, of how she was right now, of his son, in whose existence he was trying to train himself to believe. The whole world of woman, which had taken on a new value he'd never suspected since his marriage, was now lifted so high that he could not fit it into his imagination. He heard them talking about yesterday's dinner at the club, and he was thinking: "What's happening with her right now? Is she asleep? How is she? What's she thinking about? Is he crying, my son Dmitri?" And right in the middle of the conversation, in the middle of a sentence, he jumped up and left the room.
"Send word if I can see her," the prince called after him.
"Of course, in a minute," Levin answered, and without slowing down he went to her room.
She was not asleep. She was talking quietly with her mother, making plans for the christening.

Carefully tidied, her hair brushed, in a smart little cap with a touch of blue in it, her arms out on the quilt, she was lying on her back. As his eyes met hers, her eyes drew him to her. Her face, already bright, brightened more as he came closer. There was the same change in it from earthly to unearthly that you see in the face of the dead. But there it means farewell; here it meant welcome. Again a rush of feeling, like the one he had felt at the moment of the child's birth, flooded his heart. She took his hand and asked whether he had slept. He could not answer, and turned away, struggling with how weak he felt.
"I had a nap, Kostya!" she said. "And I'm so comfortable now."
She looked at him, then suddenly her expression changed.
"Give him to me," she said, hearing the baby's cry. "Give him to me, Lizaveta Petrovna, so his papa can look at him."

"Of course, his papa shall look at him," said Lizaveta Petrovna, getting up and bringing over something red and odd and wriggling. "Wait a moment, we'll get him tidy first," — and Lizaveta Petrovna laid the red, wobbling thing down on the bed, untied and retied the baby, lifting him and turning him over with one finger and dusting him with something.

Looking at the tiny, pitiful creature, Levin made a real effort to find in himself any trace of fatherly feeling for it. He felt nothing for it but disgust. But when it was undressed and he caught a glimpse of the wee, wee, little hands, the little feet, saffron-colored, with their little toes and even a little big toe distinct from the rest, and when he watched Lizaveta Petrovna fold the wide-spread little hands shut, as if they were soft springs, and slip them into linen clothes, such pity for the little creature came over him, and such terror that she would hurt it, that he caught her hand to stop her.
Lizaveta Petrovna laughed.
"Don't worry, don't worry!"

When the baby had been put right and turned into a firm little doll, Lizaveta Petrovna bounced him a bit as if proud of her handiwork and stood back a little so that Levin could see his son in all his glory.
Kitty looked sideways the same way, never taking her eyes off the baby. "Give him to me! Give him to me!" she said, and made as if to sit up.
"What are you doing, Katerina Alexandrovna? You can't move like that! Wait a moment. I'll give him to you. There — we're showing papa what a fine little fellow we are!"

And Lizaveta Petrovna, with one hand supporting the wobbling head, lifted the strange, limp, red creature in the crook of her other arm — its head almost lost in its swaddling. But it did have a nose, and slanted eyes, and smacking lips.
"A splendid baby!" said Lizaveta Petrovna.
Levin sighed with mortification. This splendid baby stirred nothing in him but disgust and pity. It was not what he had been expecting to feel at all.
He turned away while Lizaveta Petrovna held the baby to the unfamiliar breast.
Suddenly laughter made him look round. The baby had taken the breast.
"Come now, that's enough, that's enough!" said Lizaveta Petrovna, but Kitty would not let the baby go. He fell asleep in her arms.
"Look, now," said Kitty, turning the baby so he could see. The old-looking little face puckered up still more and the baby sneezed.

Smiling, barely holding back tears, Levin kissed his wife and walked out of the dark room. What he felt for this little creature was not at all what he had been expecting. There was nothing cheerful or jubilant in the feeling; on the contrary, it was a new kind of anguish. It was the awareness of a new area of exposure to pain. And that awareness was so painful at first, the fear that this helpless creature might come to harm so sharp, that it kept him from registering the strange surge of senseless joy and even pride he had felt when the baby sneezed.

title: Chapter 17
paragraphs: Stepan Arkadyevitch's affairs were in very bad shape.

The money from two-thirds of the forest had already been spent, and he had borrowed against almost all the remaining third from the merchant in advance, at a ten-percent discount. The merchant wouldn't lend any more — especially since Darya Alexandrovna, asserting her right to her own property for the first time that winter, had refused to sign the receipt for payment on the last third of the forest. All his salary went on running the household and paying off small debts that couldn't be put off any longer. There was simply no money.

It was unpleasant and uncomfortable, and in Stepan Arkadyevitch's opinion things could not go on this way. The explanation, as he saw it, was that his salary was too small. The post he held had been a really good one five years ago, but it wasn't anymore.
Petrov, the bank director, was making twelve thousand; Sventitsky, a company director, was making seventeen thousand; Mitin, who had founded a bank, was getting fifty thousand.

"Clearly I've been napping, and they've overlooked me," Stepan Arkadyevitch thought of himself. So he started keeping his eyes and ears open, and by the end of winter he had found a very good berth, and was making plans of attack — first from Moscow, through aunts, uncles, and friends, and then, when the thing was well in motion, in spring, he went to Petersburg himself. It was one of those snug, lucrative posts that there are far more of now than there used to be, with incomes anywhere from a thousand to fifty thousand roubles. It was the position of secretary to the committee of the merged agency of the southern railways and certain banking companies. Like all such posts, it called for so much energy and such a varied combination of qualifications that it was hard to find them all united in any single man. And since a man with all of them was simply not to be found, it was at least better that the post go to an honest man than to a dishonest one. And Stepan Arkadyevitch was not merely an honest man — unemphatically — in the everyday sense, he was an honest man — emphatically — in the special sense the word carries in Moscow, where they speak of an "honest" politician, an "honest" writer, an "honest" newspaper, an "honest" institution, an "honest" tendency — meaning not just that the man or institution isn't crooked, but that they are capable, on occasion, of taking a line of their own against the authorities.
Stepan Arkadyevitch moved in those Moscow circles where the word had taken on that meaning, where he was considered an honest man, and so had more claim to the appointment than other people.

The post brought in seven to ten thousand a year, and Oblonsky could hold it without resigning his government job. It was in the hands of two ministers, one lady, and two Jews; the way had already been smoothed with all of them, but Stepan Arkadyevitch still had to go to Petersburg to see them. On top of that, Stepan Arkadyevitch had promised his sister Anna that he would get a definite answer from Karenin on the question of divorce. So, borrowing fifty roubles from Dolly, he set off for Petersburg.

Stepan Arkadyevitch was sitting in Karenin's study, listening to his report on the causes of the unsatisfactory state of Russian finance, and just waiting for the moment when he would finish so he could bring up his own business or Anna.

"Yes, that's perfectly true," he said, when Alexey Alexandrovitch took off the pince-nez he could no longer read without and looked up inquiringly at his former brother-in-law. "That's perfectly true in particular cases — but the principle of our day is still freedom."

"Yes, but I am setting forth another principle, which encompasses the principle of freedom," said Alexey Alexandrovitch, stressing the word "encompasses," and he put his pince-nez back on so he could read out the passage in which this idea was stated. And turning the pages of his beautifully written, wide-margined manuscript, Alexey Alexandrovitch read the conclusive passage aloud once more.

"I am not arguing for protection on behalf of private interests, but for the public good, and for the lower and upper classes equally," he said, looking at Oblonsky over his pince-nez. "But _they_ can't grasp that — _they_ are taken up with personal interests now, and swept away by slogans."

Stepan Arkadyevitch knew that when Karenin began talking about what _they_ were doing and thinking — those people who wouldn't accept his report and were responsible for everything wrong with Russia — it meant the speech was nearly over. So now he eagerly dropped the principle of free trade and agreed entirely. Alexey Alexandrovitch paused, thoughtfully turning the pages of his manuscript.

"Oh, by the way," said Stepan Arkadyevitch, "I wanted to ask you — next time you see Pomorsky, drop him a hint that I'd be very glad to get that new appointment, secretary of the committee for the merged agency of the southern railways and the banking companies." Stepan Arkadyevitch was familiar by now with the title of the post he was after, and he rattled it off without stumbling.

Alexey Alexandrovitch asked him about the duties of this new committee, and thought it over. He was working out whether the new committee might in some way be acting against the views he had been advocating. But since the influence of the new committee was complicated and his own views had very wide application, he couldn't settle the question straight off, so he took off his pince-nez and said:
"Of course, I can mention it to him. But what exactly is your reason for wanting the appointment?"
"It's a good salary — up to nine thousand — and my circumstances...."

"Nine thousand!" Alexey Alexandrovitch repeated, and frowned. That high figure made him reflect that, on that count, Stepan Arkadyevitch's proposed post ran counter to the main tendency of his own reform projects, which always tended toward economy.
"I have argued, and have set out my views in a memorandum on the subject, that in our day these enormous salaries are evidence of the unsound economic _assiette_ of our finances."
"But what can you do?" said Stepan Arkadyevitch. "Suppose a bank director makes ten thousand — well, he's worth it. Or an engineer takes home twenty thousand — it's a growing field, after all!"

"My position is that a salary is the price paid for a commodity, and it ought to follow the law of supply and demand. If the salary is fixed with no regard for that law — as when I see, say, two engineers leaving college together, equally well-trained and capable, and one gets forty thousand while the other settles for two; or when I see lawyers and hussars, with no special qualifications, appointed directors of banking companies with vast salaries — then I conclude that the salary is not fixed according to supply and demand, but simply by personal influence. And that is a grave abuse in itself, and one that has bad effects on the government service. I argue...."
Stepan Arkadyevitch hurried to cut his brother-in-law off.

"Yes — but you must agree this is a new institution of unquestioned usefulness that's being set up. After all, it's a growing thing! What they especially insist on is that it be run honestly," Stepan Arkadyevitch said with emphasis.
But the Moscow weight of the word "honest" was lost on Alexey Alexandrovitch.
"Honesty is only a negative qualification," he said.
"Well, you'll do me a great service in any case," said Stepan Arkadyevitch, "by putting in a word with Pomorsky — just in the course of conversation...."
"But I think it's more in Volgarinov's hands," said Alexey Alexandrovitch.

"Volgarinov has signed on, as far as he's concerned," said Stepan Arkadyevitch, turning red. He had reddened at the mention of the name, because that morning he had been at the Jew Volgarinov's, and the visit had left a bad taste.

Stepan Arkadyevitch firmly believed that the committee he was angling to join was a new, genuine, and honest public body, but that morning, when Volgarinov had — deliberately, no question — kept him waiting two hours along with other petitioners in his anteroom, he had suddenly felt uneasy.

Whether it was that he, a descendant of Rurik, Prince Oblonsky, had been kept waiting two hours to see a Jew, or that for the first time in his life he wasn't following his ancestors' example by serving the government but was branching off into a new line of work, either way he was very uncomfortable. During those two hours in Volgarinov's anteroom, Stepan Arkadyevitch — strolling jauntily about the room, tugging at his whiskers, falling into conversation with the other petitioners, and composing an epigram on his own situation — was hard at work hiding from the others, and even from himself, the feeling he was experiencing.

But the whole time he was uncomfortable and angry, and could not have said why — whether because he couldn't get his epigram quite right, or for some other reason. When Volgarinov had finally received him with exaggerated politeness and unmistakable triumph at his humiliation, and had all but refused him the favor, Stepan Arkadyevitch had been quick to push the whole thing out of his mind as fast as possible. And now, at the mere memory, he blushed.

title: Chapter 18
paragraphs: "Now there's something else I want to talk about, and you know what it is. About Anna," Stepan Arkadyevitch said, after a brief pause, shaking off the unpleasant memory.
The moment Oblonsky said Anna's name, Alexey Alexandrovitch's face changed completely; all the life went out of it, and it looked weary and dead.
"What exactly do you want from me?" he said, shifting in his chair and snapping his pince-nez shut.

"A definite settlement, Alexey Alexandrovitch — some kind of settlement of the situation. I'm appealing to you" ("not as an injured husband," Stepan Arkadyevitch was about to say, but afraid of wrecking his case with that, he changed it) "not as a statesman" (which didn't quite fit, _à propos_), "but simply as a man, and a good-hearted man and a Christian. You must take pity on her," he said.
"Meaning what, precisely?" Karenin said softly.
"Pity, yes. If you had seen her, as I have — I've been spending all winter with her — you would pity her. Her position is dreadful, just dreadful!"
"I had imagined," answered Alexey Alexandrovitch, his voice rising almost to a shrill pitch, "that Anna Arkadyevna had everything she wanted for herself."
"Oh, Alexey Alexandrovitch — for heaven's sake, let's not start trading reproaches! What's past is past, and you know what she wants and is waiting for — a divorce."

"But I believe Anna Arkadyevna refuses a divorce if I make it a condition that she leave me my son. I answered her on that basis, and I assumed the matter was closed. I consider it closed," Alexey Alexandrovitch said sharply.

"For heaven's sake, don't get heated!" Stepan Arkadyevitch said, touching his brother-in-law's knee. "The matter is not closed. Let me lay it out again. When you parted, you were as generous as anyone could possibly have been; you were ready to give her everything — freedom, even a divorce. She felt that. No, don't doubt it — she did feel it, to such a degree that in the first moment, conscious of how she had wronged you, she didn't and couldn't take everything into account. She gave it all up. But experience, and time, have shown that her position is unbearable, impossible."
"Anna Arkadyevna's life can be of no interest to me," Alexey Alexandrovitch put in, raising his eyebrows.

"Allow me not to believe that," Stepan Arkadyevitch answered gently. "Her position is intolerable for her, and benefits no one. She'll say she deserves it — you'll say so. She knows that, and she's asking nothing of you; she says plainly that she dare not ask. But I — all of us, her relatives, everyone who loves her — we are begging you, imploring you. Why must she suffer? Who is any better off for it?"
"Excuse me, but you seem to be putting me in the position of the guilty party," observed Alexey Alexandrovitch.

"Oh, no — oh, no, not at all! Please understand me," said Stepan Arkadyevitch, touching his hand again, as though sure that this physical contact would soften his brother-in-law. "All I'm saying is this: her situation is intolerable, you have the power to ease it, and you lose nothing by it. I'll arrange everything for you, so that you don't notice it. You did promise it, you know."

"The promise was given before. And I had supposed the question of my son had settled the matter. Besides, I had hoped Anna Arkadyevna had enough generosity...." Alexey Alexandrovitch got the words out with difficulty, his lips twitching and his face pale.

"She leaves it all to your generosity. She begs, she implores one thing of you — to free her from the impossible position she is in. She is not asking for her son now. Alexey Alexandrovitch, you are a good man. Put yourself in her place for a minute. The question of divorce, for her, in her position, is a matter of life and death. If you had never promised it, she would have made her peace with her position, she would have stayed living in the country. But you promised it, and she wrote to you, and she moved to Moscow. And here she's been for six months in Moscow, every chance encounter cutting her to the quick, every day waiting for an answer. It's like keeping a condemned criminal six months with the rope around his neck, promising him either death or mercy. Have pity on her, and I will undertake to arrange everything. _Vos scrupules_...."
"I'm not talking about that, not that...." Alexey Alexandrovitch broke in with disgust. "But perhaps I promised what I had no right to promise."
"So you're taking back your promise?"
"I have never refused to do what is possible, but I want time to consider how much of what I promised is possible."
"No, Alexey Alexandrovitch!" Oblonsky cried, jumping up. "I won't believe that! She's as unhappy as only an unhappy woman can be, and you cannot refuse in such...."
"As much of what I promised as is possible. _Vous professez d'être libre penseur._ But as a believer I cannot, in a matter of such gravity, act in violation of the Christian law."
"But in Christian societies, and in ours so far as I know, divorce is permitted," said Stepan Arkadyevitch. "Divorce is sanctioned by our church, even. And we see...."
"It's allowed, but not in the sense...."

"Alexey Alexandrovitch, you don't sound like yourself," Oblonsky said after a brief pause. "Wasn't it you (and didn't all of us admire you for it?) who forgave everything, and, moved purely by Christian feeling, was ready to make any sacrifice? You said yourself: if a man takes thy coat, give him thy cloak also — and now...."
"I beg you," Alexey Alexandrovitch said shrilly, suddenly springing to his feet, his face white, his jaw twitching, "I beg you to drop this — to drop this subject!"

"Oh, no — oh, forgive me, forgive me if I've hurt you," Stepan Arkadyevitch said, holding out his hand with an embarrassed smile. "I'm only the messenger; I was simply delivering the message that had been given to me."
Alexey Alexandrovitch gave him his hand, thought for a moment, and said:
"I must think it over and seek guidance. The day after tomorrow I'll give you a final answer," he said, after another moment of thought.

title: Chapter 19
paragraphs: Stepan Arkadyevitch was on the point of leaving when Korney came in to announce:
"Sergey Alexyevitch!"
"Who's Sergey Alexyevitch?" Stepan Arkadyevitch was beginning, but he caught himself at once.
"Ah, Seryozha!" he said out loud. "Sergey Alexyevitch! I thought it was the head of a department. Anna asked me to see him too," he thought.

And he recalled the timid, pleading expression with which Anna had said to him at parting, "Anyway, you'll see him. Find out exactly where he is, who's looking after him. And Stiva... if it were possible! Could it be possible?" Stepan Arkadyevitch knew what was meant by that "if it were possible" — if it were possible to work the divorce out so she could have her son.... Stepan Arkadyevitch saw now that it was no use dreaming about that, but he was still glad to see his nephew.
Alexey Alexandrovitch reminded his brother-in-law that they never spoke to the boy about his mother, and asked him not to mention a single word about her.

"He was very ill after that meeting with his mother, which we hadn't foreseen," Alexey Alexandrovitch said. "In fact, we feared for his life. But with proper treatment and sea-bathing in the summer, he got his strength back, and now, on the doctor's advice, I have let him go to school. And the companionship of school has certainly done him good. He's perfectly well, and making good progress."

"What a fine young fellow he's grown into! Not Seryozha anymore — fully Sergey Alexyevitch!" said Stepan Arkadyevitch, smiling, looking at the handsome, broad-shouldered boy in a blue jacket and long trousers who came in briskly and confidently. The boy looked healthy and good-natured. He bowed to his uncle as to a stranger, but recognizing him, he flushed and turned away quickly, as though offended and annoyed by something. He went up to his father and handed him a slip with the marks he had earned at school.
"Well, that's quite respectable," said his father. "You may go."
"He's thinner and taller — he's grown out of being a child and into being a boy. I like that," said Stepan Arkadyevitch. "Do you remember me?"
The boy glanced quickly back at his uncle.
"Yes, _mon oncle_," he answered, glancing at his father, and looked down again.
His uncle called him over and took his hand.
"Well, and how are you getting on?" he said, wanting to talk to him, and not knowing what to say.

The boy, blushing and giving no answer, carefully pulled his hand free. As soon as Stepan Arkadyevitch let go of his hand, he glanced uncertainly at his father, and like a bird set loose, darted out of the room.

A year had gone by since the last time Seryozha had seen his mother. Since then he'd heard nothing more about her. And in the course of that year he had started school and made friends with his schoolmates. The dreams and memories of his mother, which had made him ill after he had seen her, did not occupy his thoughts anymore. When they did come back, he deliberately pushed them away, treating them as shameful and girlish — beneath the dignity of a boy and a schoolboy. He knew that his father and his mother were separated by some quarrel, he knew that he had to stay with his father, and he tried to get used to the idea.

He disliked seeing his uncle, who looked so much like his mother, because it stirred up the very memories he was ashamed of. He disliked it all the more because, from a few words he had caught while waiting at the study door, and even more from the looks on his father's and his uncle's faces, he had guessed that they must have been talking about his mother. So, not to start condemning the father he lived with and depended on, and above all not to give in to sentimentality, which he considered so demeaning, Seryozha tried not to look at this uncle who had come to disturb his peace of mind, and not to think about what the uncle had brought up in him.

But when Stepan Arkadyevitch, coming out after him, caught sight of him on the stairs and called him over and asked how he spent his recess at school, Seryozha talked more freely with him, out of his father's presence.

"We have a railway now," he said in answer to his uncle's question. "It works like this, you see: two of us sit on a bench — those are the passengers — and one stands up straight on the bench. And we're all harnessed to it by our arms or our belts, and we run through all the rooms — the doors get left open in advance. Well, and it's pretty hard work being the conductor!"
"That's the one who stands?" Stepan Arkadyevitch asked, smiling.
"Yes — and you need nerve for it, and quick wits, especially when they stop all of a sudden, or someone falls down."

"Yes, that must be a serious business," Stepan Arkadyevitch said, watching with a sad sort of interest those eager eyes, so like his mother's — not childish anymore, not entirely innocent now. And although he had promised Alexey Alexandrovitch not to talk about Anna, he couldn't hold himself back.
"Do you remember your mother?" he asked suddenly.

"No, I don't," Seryozha said quickly. He flushed crimson, and his face clouded over. And his uncle couldn't get anything more out of him. The tutor found his pupil on the stairs half an hour later, and for a long time couldn't tell whether the boy was sulking or crying.
"What's the matter? I expect you hurt yourself when you fell down?" the tutor said. "I told you it was a dangerous game. We'll have to mention it to the director."
"If I had hurt myself, no one would have known. That's for sure."
"Well, what is it then?"
"Leave me alone! Whether I remember or whether I don't — what business is it of his? Why should I have to remember? Leave me in peace!" he said, addressing not the tutor but the whole world.

title: Chapter 20
paragraphs: Stepan Arkadyevitch, as usual, didn't waste his time in Petersburg. While he was there, besides business, his sister's divorce, and the coveted appointment, he wanted, as he always did, to freshen himself up, as he put it, after the mustiness of Moscow.

Despite its _cafés chantants_ and its omnibuses, Moscow was still a stagnant bog. Stepan Arkadyevitch always felt it. After spending some time in Moscow, especially in close contact with his family, he was aware of a drop in his spirits. After being in Moscow a long stretch without a break, he reached the point of seriously starting to worry about his wife's irritability and reproaches, his children's health and schooling, the petty details of his work at the office — even his being in debt began to weigh on him.
