But all he had to do was go and spend a little while in Petersburg, in the circles he moved in there, where people lived — really lived — instead of merely vegetating as in Moscow, and any such thoughts vanished and melted away at once, like wax in front of a fire. His wife?... Just that day he'd been talking to Prince Tchetchensky. Prince Tchetchensky had a wife and a family — grown-up sons as pages in the corps — and he also had a separate illegitimate family of children. The first family was very nice too, but Prince Tchetchensky felt happier with his second family; and he used to take his eldest son along to visit the second family, and he told Stepan Arkadyevitch he thought it was good for the son, broadened his mind. What would they have said about that in Moscow?

His children? In Petersburg, children didn't keep their parents from enjoying life. Children were brought up in schools, and there was no trace of the bizarre idea you saw in Moscow — in Lvov's household, for instance — that all of life's pleasures were for the children, while the parents had only work and worry. Here people understood that a man is duty-bound to live for himself, the way every cultivated man should.

His official duties? Office work here wasn't the stiff, hopeless grind it was in Moscow. Here there was something interesting in official life. A chance meeting, a favor done, a clever phrase, a knack for funny impressions, and a man's career could be made in no time. So it had gone with Bryantsev, whom Stepan Arkadyevitch had met the day before, and who was now one of the top officials in government. That kind of official work was worth doing.

Petersburg's attitude on money matters had a particularly soothing effect on Stepan Arkadyevitch. Bartnyansky — who, judging by the style he lived in, must spend at least fifty thousand — had made an interesting remark about it the day before.
As they were talking before dinner, Stepan Arkadyevitch said to Bartnyansky:
"You're on good terms with Mordvinsky, I think; could you do me a favor — put in a word for me with him. There's an appointment I'd like to land — secretary of the agency...."
"Oh, I won't remember any of that even if you tell me.... But what possesses you to get mixed up with railways and Jews?... However you look at it, it's a low business."
Stepan Arkadyevitch didn't tell Bartnyansky that it was "a growing thing" — Bartnyansky wouldn't have got it.
"I need the money. I've got nothing to live on."
"You're living, aren't you?"
"Yes — but in debt."
"Are you really? A lot?" said Bartnyansky sympathetically.
"Quite a lot — twenty thousand."
Bartnyansky burst out into good-humored laughter.
"Oh, lucky man!" he said. "My debts run to a million and a half, and I have nothing, and yet I live — as you can see!"

And Stepan Arkadyevitch saw that this was true not just in words but in fact. Zhivahov owed three hundred thousand, didn't have a kopeck to his name, and lived — and lived in style too. Count Krivtsov was considered a hopeless case by everyone, and yet he kept two mistresses. Petrovsky had blown through five millions, and still lived in just the same style, and was even a manager in the finance department on a salary of twenty thousand. But beyond all that, Petersburg had a physically agreeable effect on Stepan Arkadyevitch. It made him younger. In Moscow he sometimes found a grey hair in his head, dropped off to sleep after dinner, stretched, climbed the stairs slowly with heavy breathing, was bored by the company of young women, and didn't dance at balls. In Petersburg he always felt ten years younger.
His experience in Petersburg was just what Prince Pyotr Oblonsky, a man of sixty just back from abroad, had described to him the day before:

"We don't know how to live here," Pyotr Oblonsky said. "I spent the summer in Baden, and you wouldn't believe it, I felt like a young man again. A glimpse of a pretty woman, and my thoughts.... You dine and drink a glass of wine, and you feel strong and ready for anything. I came home to Russia — had to see my wife, and on top of that go down to my country place — and there, you'd hardly believe it, in a fortnight I was in a dressing gown and had stopped dressing for dinner. No need to say I had no thoughts left for pretty women. I'd become quite an old gentleman. There was nothing left for me but to think about my eternal salvation. I went off to Paris — and I was right as rain at once."

Stepan Arkadyevitch felt exactly the difference Pyotr Oblonsky had described. In Moscow he degenerated so much that, if he'd had to stay there for any long stretch, he might in earnest have come round to thinking about his salvation; in Petersburg he felt himself a man of the world again.

Between Princess Betsy Tverskaya and Stepan Arkadyevitch there had long been a rather peculiar arrangement. Stepan Arkadyevitch always flirted with her in jest, and used to say to her, also in jest, the most improper things, knowing that nothing pleased her so much. The day after his conversation with Karenin, Stepan Arkadyevitch went to see her, and felt so young that in this teasing flirtation and nonsense he recklessly went so far that he didn't know how to extract himself, since unluckily he was so far from being attracted to her that he found her actually unpleasant. What made it hard to change the subject was that he was very attractive to her. So he was considerably relieved when Princess Myakaya arrived and cut short their _tête-à-tête_.

"Ah, so you're here!" she said when she saw him. "Well, and how is your poor sister? Don't look at me like that," she added. "Ever since they all turned against her — all those people a thousand times worse than she is — I've thought she did a very fine thing. I can't forgive Vronsky for not letting me know when she was in Petersburg. I would have gone to see her, and gone everywhere with her. Please give her my love. Come, tell me about her."

"Yes, her position is very difficult; she...." Stepan Arkadyevitch began, in the simplicity of his heart taking Princess Myakaya's "tell me about her" at face value. Princess Myakaya interrupted him immediately, as she always did, and started talking herself.

"She's done what everyone else does, except me — only they hide it. But she wouldn't be deceitful, and she did a fine thing. And she did even better in throwing over that crazy brother-in-law of yours. You'll have to excuse me. Everyone used to say he was so clever, so terribly clever. I was the only one who said he was a fool. Now that he's gone in so deep with Lidia Ivanovna and Landau, everyone's saying he's mad — and I would normally prefer not to agree with everybody, but this time I can't help it."

"Oh, please, explain it to me," said Stepan Arkadyevitch. "What does it all mean? Yesterday I went to see him on my sister's behalf, and asked him for a final answer. He gave me no answer, and said he would think it over. But this morning, instead of an answer, I got an invitation from Countess Lidia Ivanovna for this evening."
"Ah, so that's it, that's it!" said Princess Myakaya gleefully. "They're going to ask Landau what he should say."
"Ask Landau? Why? Who or what is Landau?"

"What — you don't know Jules Landau, _le fameux Jules Landau, le clairvoyant_? He's mad too, but your sister's fate depends on him. See what comes of living in the provinces — you don't know anything about anything. Landau, you see, was a _commis_ in a shop in Paris, and he went to see a doctor; and in the doctor's waiting room he fell asleep, and in his sleep he started giving advice to all the patients. And remarkable advice it was, too. Then the wife of Yury Meledinsky — you know, the invalid? — heard of this Landau, and brought him in to see her husband. And he cured the husband, though I can't say I see he did him much good, since he's just as feeble a creature as ever, but they believed in him, and they took him along with them and brought him to Russia. Here everyone has rushed to him, and he's begun doctoring everyone. He cured Countess Bezzubova, and she took such a fancy to him that she adopted him."
"Adopted him?"

"Yes, as her son. He isn't Landau anymore now, but Count Bezzubov. Anyway, that's neither here nor there; but Lidia — and I'm fond of her, but she has a screw loose somewhere — has lost her heart to this Landau, and nothing is decided now in her house or Alexey Alexandrovitch's without him. So your sister's fate is now in the hands of Landau, _alias_ Count Bezzubov."

title: Chapter 21
paragraphs: After an excellent dinner and a great deal of cognac at Bartnyansky's, Stepan Arkadyevitch arrived at Countess Lidia Ivanovna's only a little later than the agreed hour.

"Who else is with the countess — a Frenchman?" Stepan Arkadyevitch asked the hall-porter, glancing at Alexey Alexandrovitch's familiar overcoat and at another strange, rather artless-looking coat fitted with clasps.
"Alexey Alexandrovitch Karenin and Count Bezzubov," the porter answered gravely.

"Princess Myakaya guessed right," Stepan Arkadyevitch thought as he climbed the stairs. "Curious! Still, it might be useful to get on good terms with her. She has enormous influence. A single word from her to Pomorsky and the appointment would be in the bag."

Outside it was still broad daylight, but in Countess Lidia Ivanovna's little drawing-room the blinds were down and the lamps were lit. At a round table beneath a lamp sat the countess and Alexey Alexandrovitch, talking in low voices. A short, slight, very pale and handsome man, with feminine hips, knock-kneed legs, fine glittering eyes, and long hair lying against the collar of his coat, stood at the far end of the room studying the portraits on the wall. After greeting the lady of the house and Alexey Alexandrovitch, Stepan Arkadyevitch could not keep from stealing another look at the stranger.
"Monsieur Landau!" the countess said to him, with a softness and a care that struck Oblonsky. And she made the introductions.

Landau turned quickly, came over, and with a smile laid his moist, lifeless hand in Stepan Arkadyevitch's outstretched one, then walked away again and went back to gazing at the portraits. The countess and Alexey Alexandrovitch exchanged a meaningful look.
"I'm very glad you came, especially today," said Countess Lidia Ivanovna, motioning Stepan Arkadyevitch to a seat next to Karenin.

"I introduced him to you as Landau," she said quietly, glancing at the Frenchman and then immediately at Alexey Alexandrovitch, "but he is really Count Bezzubov, as you probably know. Only he doesn't care for the title."
"Yes, so I've heard," Stepan Arkadyevitch answered. "They say he made a complete cure of Countess Bezzubova."
"She was here today, poor thing!" the countess said, turning to Alexey Alexandrovitch. "This separation is dreadful for her. It's such a blow!"
"And he's definitely going?" Alexey Alexandrovitch asked.
"Yes, to Paris. He heard a voice yesterday," Countess Lidia Ivanovna said, with a glance at Stepan Arkadyevitch.
"Ah, a voice!" Oblonsky repeated, feeling he must move as carefully as possible in a circle where something unusual was either happening or about to happen, and to which he had no key.
A pause followed; then Countess Lidia Ivanovna, as though coming to the main subject, turned to Oblonsky with a delicate smile.

"I have known about you for a long time, and I'm very glad to get to know you better. _Les amis de nos amis sont nos amis._ But to be a true friend, one has to enter into the spiritual condition of one's friend, and I'm afraid you are not doing that with Alexey Alexandrovitch. You see what I mean?" she said, raising her fine, thoughtful eyes.
"In part, countess, I understand Alexey Alexandrovitch's position...." Oblonsky said. Having no real idea what they were driving at, he meant to keep to vague generalities.

"The change is not in his outward position," Countess Lidia Ivanovna said sternly, her loving eyes following Alexey Alexandrovitch as he rose and walked over to Landau. "His heart has been changed, a new heart has been granted to him, and I'm afraid you don't fully grasp the change that has taken place in him."

"Well, in broad terms I can picture the change. We've always been on good terms, and now...." Stepan Arkadyevitch said, answering the countess's expression with a sympathetic glance and trying meanwhile to work out which of the two ministers she was on the closer footing with, so as to know which one to ask her to put in a word for him.

"The change that has taken place in him cannot reduce his love for his neighbors; on the contrary, that change can only deepen the love in his heart. But I'm afraid you don't follow me. Won't you have some tea?" she said, signaling with her eyes to the footman who was offering tea on a tray.
"Not quite, countess. Of course, his misfortune...."
"Yes, a misfortune that has turned into the highest happiness, the moment his heart was made new and filled to the brim with it," she said, looking at Stepan Arkadyevitch with eyes full of love.
"I really think I might ask her to speak to both of them," Stepan Arkadyevitch thought.
"Of course, countess," he said aloud, "but I imagine that changes of that kind are so private a matter that no one — not even the closest friend — likes to talk about them."
"On the contrary! We ought to speak openly and help each other."
"Yes, no doubt, but there are such differences of conviction, and besides...." Oblonsky said with a gentle smile.
"There can be no difference where it's a question of holy truth."
"Oh, no, of course, but...." Stepan Arkadyevitch broke off, embarrassed. He grasped at last that the subject was religion.
"I have a feeling he'll fall asleep any moment," Alexey Alexandrovitch murmured significantly, going over to Lidia Ivanovna.

Stepan Arkadyevitch looked over. Landau was sitting at the window, his elbow on the chair-back, his head sagging. Noticing the eyes turned on him, he raised it and gave a smile of childlike innocence.

"Pay no attention," Lidia Ivanovna said, and she lightly pushed a chair into place for Alexey Alexandrovitch. "I've noticed...." she began, when a footman came in with a letter. Lidia Ivanovna ran her eyes rapidly over the note, excused herself, dashed off a reply with extraordinary speed, handed it to the man, and came back to the table. "I've noticed," she went on, "that Moscow people, especially the men, are more indifferent to religion than anyone."
"Oh, no, countess, I'd have thought the people of Moscow had the reputation of being the steadiest in the faith," Stepan Arkadyevitch answered.
"But as far as I can tell, you yourself are unfortunately among the indifferent," Alexey Alexandrovitch said, turning to him with a weary smile.
"How can anyone be indifferent!" Lidia Ivanovna exclaimed.
"I'm not so much indifferent on that subject as waiting in suspense," Stepan Arkadyevitch said with his most disarming smile. "I hardly think the time for such questions has come for me yet."
Alexey Alexandrovitch and Lidia Ivanovna exchanged a look.

"We can never tell whether the time has come for us or not," Alexey Alexandrovitch said sternly. "We should not be thinking about whether we are ready or not. God's grace doesn't work by human reasoning: sometimes it doesn't come to those who strive for it, and comes instead to those who are unprepared, as it did to Saul."
"No, I think it won't be just yet," said Lidia Ivanovna, who had meanwhile been watching the Frenchman's movements. Landau stood up and came over to them.
"May I listen?" he asked.
"Yes, of course; I didn't want to disturb you," Lidia Ivanovna said, gazing at him tenderly. "Sit here with us."
"One only has to keep one's eyes open to let in the light," Alexey Alexandrovitch went on.
"Ah, if you knew the happiness we know, feeling His presence in our hearts at every moment!" said Countess Lidia Ivanovna with a rapturous smile.

"But a man may sometimes feel unworthy of rising to such a height," said Stepan Arkadyevitch, conscious of the hypocrisy of conceding this religious altitude, but unable to bring himself to confess his free-thinking views in front of someone who, with one word to Pomorsky, could secure him the post he so badly wanted.

"You mean that sin holds him back?" said Lidia Ivanovna. "That is a false notion. There is no sin for those who believe; their sin has been atoned for. _Pardon,_" she added, glancing at the footman, who had come in again with another letter. She read it and gave her answer aloud: "Tomorrow at the Grand Duchess's, say." "For the believer, sin is not," she went on.
"Yes, but faith without works is dead," Stepan Arkadyevitch said, fishing up the line from the catechism and clinging to his independence only by his smile.

"There — straight out of the epistle of St. James," Alexey Alexandrovitch said to Lidia Ivanovna, with a touch of reproach in his voice. It was clearly a topic they had been over more than once. "What damage has been done by the false reading of that passage! Nothing keeps men back from belief more than that misreading. 'I have no works, so I cannot believe,' though that is never actually said. The very opposite is what is said."

"Striving toward God, saving one's soul by fasting," said Countess Lidia Ivanovna with a kind of disgusted contempt, "those are the crude ideas of our monks.... And yet that is nowhere stated. It's far simpler and easier than that," she added, looking at Oblonsky with the same encouraging smile she used at court to put nervous young maids of honor at their ease in unfamiliar surroundings.
"We are saved by Christ, who suffered for us. We are saved by faith," Alexey Alexandrovitch put in, with an approving glance at her.
_"Vous comprenez l'anglais?"_ Lidia Ivanovna asked, and on hearing that he did, she got up and went over to a shelf of books.

"I'd like to read him 'Safe and Happy,' or 'Under the Wing,'" she said, looking inquiringly at Karenin. And finding the book, she sat down again in her place and opened it. "It's very short. It describes the way faith can be reached, and the happiness, beyond all earthly joy, that it brings into the soul. The believer cannot be unhappy, because he is not alone. You'll see." She was just settling herself to read when the footman appeared once more. "Madame Borozdina? Tell her, tomorrow at two o'clock. Yes," she said, keeping her finger in her place in the book and gazing into space with her fine, thoughtful eyes. "That is how true faith acts. You know Marie Sanina? You've heard what happened to her? She lost her only child. She was in despair. And then what? She found this comforter, and she now thanks God for the death of her child. Such is the happiness faith brings!"

"Oh, yes, that is very...." said Stepan Arkadyevitch, glad they were finally going to read so that he could pull himself together. "No, I see I'd better not ask her anything today," he thought. "If I can just escape this without putting my foot in it!"
"It will be dull for you," Countess Lidia Ivanovna said, addressing Landau. "You don't know English, but it's short."
"Oh, I shall understand," Landau said, with the same smile, and closed his eyes. Alexey Alexandrovitch and Lidia Ivanovna exchanged meaningful looks, and the reading began.

title: Chapter 22
paragraphs: Stepan Arkadyevitch felt completely thrown by the strange talk he was hearing for the first time. As a rule, the complexity of Petersburg had a stimulating effect on him, shaking him out of his Moscow torpor. But he enjoyed and understood that complexity only in the circles he knew and felt at home in. Out of his element here, he was bewildered and rattled, and could not get his bearings. As he listened to Countess Lidia Ivanovna, aware of Landau's beautiful eyes fixed on him — artless eyes, or perhaps artful, he couldn't decide — Stepan Arkadyevitch began to feel a peculiar heaviness in his head.

The most disconnected ideas were jumbled together in his mind. "Marie Sanina is glad her child died.... A smoke would be wonderful right now!... To be saved, you only need to believe, and the monks don't know how it's done, but Countess Lidia Ivanovna does.... And why is my head so heavy? Is it the cognac, or is all this just so peculiar? Anyhow, I think I haven't done anything out of place so far. Still, it won't do to ask her now. They say they make you say your prayers. I only hope they won't make me — that would be too idiotic. And what nonsense she's reading! But her accent is good. Landau — Bezzubov — what is he Bezzubov for?" All at once Stepan Arkadyevitch realized that his lower jaw was forming an unstoppable yawn. He pulled at his whiskers to cover it and gave himself a shake. But a moment later he became aware that he was drifting off and on the verge of snoring. He came to just as Countess Lidia Ivanovna's voice was saying, "He is asleep." Stepan Arkadyevitch jerked guiltily, certain he had been caught. But he was reassured at once when he saw that "He is asleep" referred not to him but to Landau. The Frenchman was asleep, exactly as Stepan Arkadyevitch had been. But Stepan Arkadyevitch's being asleep would have offended them, he thought (though even that, he reflected, might not be true — everything here was so strange), while Landau's being asleep delighted them no end, especially Countess Lidia Ivanovna.

_"Mon ami,"_ said Lidia Ivanovna, carefully holding the folds of her silk gown so they wouldn't rustle, and in her excitement calling Karenin not Alexey Alexandrovitch but _"mon ami," "donnez-lui la main. Vous voyez?_ Sh!" she hissed at the footman as he came in again. "Not at home."

The Frenchman was asleep, or pretending to be, his head on the back of his chair, his moist hand on his knee making faint little movements, as though groping for something. Alexey Alexandrovitch got up, tried to move carefully but bumped into the table, then walked over and laid his hand in the Frenchman's. Stepan Arkadyevitch got up too, opened his eyes wide and tried to wake himself in case he was asleep, and looked from one of them to the other. It was all happening for real. Stepan Arkadyevitch felt his head growing worse and worse.
"_Que la personne qui est arrivée la dernière, celle qui demande, qu'elle sorte! Qu'elle sorte!_" the Frenchman pronounced without opening his eyes.
"_Vous m'excuserez, mais vous voyez.... Revenez vers dix heures, encore mieux demain._"
"_Qu'elle sorte!_" the Frenchman repeated impatiently.

"_C'est moi, n'est-ce pas?_" And on getting an affirmative answer, Stepan Arkadyevitch — forgetting the favor he had meant to ask of Lidia Ivanovna, forgetting his sister's affairs, caring for nothing now but the sole wish to get out as quickly as possible — tiptoed away and bolted into the street as if escaping a plague house. For a long time he chatted and joked with his cab-driver, trying to recover his nerve.

At the French theater, where he caught the last act, and afterward at the Tatar restaurant over champagne, Stepan Arkadyevitch felt himself a little restored in the atmosphere he was used to. But all the same he did not feel himself the whole evening.

On reaching the home of Pyotr Oblonsky, where he was staying, Stepan Arkadyevitch found a note from Betsy. She wrote that she was eager to finish their interrupted conversation and asked him to come the next day. He had barely read the note, frowning at its contents, when he heard below the heavy tread of servants carrying something heavy.

Stepan Arkadyevitch went out to see. It was the rejuvenated Pyotr Oblonsky. He was so drunk he couldn't manage the stairs; but when he caught sight of Stepan Arkadyevitch he ordered the servants to set him on his feet, clung to him, and walked with him into the room, where he began to recount his evening and fell asleep in the middle of it.

Stepan Arkadyevitch was in very low spirits — a rare thing for him — and for a long time he could not get to sleep. Everything he thought back on was repellent; but the most repellent of all, somehow shameful, was the memory of his evening at Countess Lidia Ivanovna's.

The next day he received a final answer from Alexey Alexandrovitch refusing to grant Anna's divorce, and he understood that the decision rested on what the Frenchman had said in his real or pretended trance.

title: Chapter 23
paragraphs: For any undertaking in family life to come off, there has to be either a complete break between husband and wife or genuine agreement between them. When the relationship is wavering — neither one thing nor the other — nothing can get done.
Many families remain stuck in the same place for years, even though both husband and wife are sick of it, simply because there is neither a real break nor real agreement between them.

Both Vronsky and Anna found life in Moscow unbearable in the heat and dust, once the spring sunshine gave way to the glare of summer, and the trees along the boulevards had long since unfurled their leaves, which were now coated with dust. But they did not go back to Vozdvizhenskoe as they had planned long ago; they went on staying in Moscow, though they both hated it, because lately there had been no agreement between them.

The irritability that kept them apart had no outward cause, and every attempt to come to an understanding only sharpened it instead of dissolving it. It was an inner friction, grounded in her conviction that his love had cooled, and in his regret that he had put himself in such a difficult position for her sake — a position that she, instead of easing, made still more difficult. Neither of them spoke their grievance out in full, but each considered the other in the wrong and seized on every excuse to prove it.

In her eyes the whole of him — his habits, his ideas, his desires, his entire spiritual and physical makeup — boiled down to one thing: love for women, and that love, she felt, ought to be focused entirely on her alone. That love had cooled; therefore, she reasoned, he must have diverted part of it to other women or to one other woman — and she was jealous. She was jealous, not of any particular woman, but of the loss itself. Lacking an object for her jealousy, she went hunting for one. At the smallest hint she shifted the jealousy from one figure to another. One moment she was jealous of the low women with whom he might so easily pick up his old bachelor ties; the next, of the society women he might meet; then of an imaginary girl he might want to marry, for whose sake he would break with her. This last form of jealousy tormented her most of all, especially since he had carelessly let slip, in a frank moment, that his mother knew him so little she had had the gall to try and persuade him to marry the young Princess Sorokina.

Being jealous, Anna was furious with him, and found reasons for fury in everything. Every hardship of her situation she blamed on him. The agonizing limbo she had endured in Moscow, Alexey Alexandrovitch's foot-dragging and indecision, her loneliness — she laid it all on him. If he had loved her, he would have seen how bitter her position was and rescued her from it. The fact that she was in Moscow and not in the country was his fault too. He could not bury himself in the country as she would have liked. He needed society, and so he had put her in this dreadful situation, the bitterness of which he refused to see. And it was again his fault that she was permanently separated from her son.

Even the rare moments of tenderness that came now and then did nothing to comfort her; in his tenderness now she could detect a tinge of complacency, of self-assurance, that hadn't been there before, and it infuriated her.

It was dusk. Anna was alone, waiting for him to come back from a bachelor dinner. She paced up and down in his study (the room least exposed to the noise from the street) and turned over every detail of their quarrel the day before. Going back from the well-remembered, offensive words to what had set it off, she finally arrived at its starting-point. For a long while she could hardly believe that the dispute had grown out of a conversation so harmless and so unimportant to either of them. But that is how it had happened. The whole thing began with his laughing at girls' high schools and declaring them useless, while she defended them. He had spoken slightingly of women's education in general, and had said that Hannah, Anna's English protégée, had not the slightest need to know any physics.

This stung Anna. She read it as a contemptuous swipe at what she was doing. She thought up a phrase to pay him back for the hurt. "I don't expect you to understand me, my feelings, the way anyone who loved me might, but I did expect ordinary tact," she said.
He had actually flushed with annoyance and said something unpleasant. She could not remember what she had answered, but at that point, with a clear wish to hurt her in return, he had said:
"I have no interest in your obsession with this girl, that's true, because I can see it isn't natural."
The cruelty with which he was smashing the world she had so painstakingly built for herself to bear her hard life, and the injustice of his accusing her of affectation, of putting it on, set her off.
"I am very sorry that only what's coarse and material is understandable and natural to you," she said, and walked out of the room.
When he came in to her last night, neither had brought up the quarrel, but both felt that the quarrel had been papered over rather than ended.

Today he had not been at home all day, and she felt so lonely and miserable in being on bad terms with him that she wanted to put it all behind her, to forgive him and make up; she wanted to take the blame on herself and let him off.
"I'm the one to blame. I'm touchy, I'm insanely jealous. I'll make it up with him and we'll go away to the country; there I'll be more at peace."

"Unnatural!" The word that had stung her most suddenly came back — not so much the word as the intent to wound that lay behind it. "I know what he meant; he meant — unnatural, not loving my own daughter, to love another person's child. What does he know about love for children, about my love for Seryozha, whom I've sacrificed for him? But that need to hurt me! No, he loves another woman, that has to be it."

And realizing that, in trying to recover her peace of mind, she had gone around the same circle she had been around so many times before and had come back to her former exasperation, she was horrified at herself. "Can it really be impossible? Can I really not control myself?" she said, and she began over again from the beginning. "He's truthful, he's honest, he loves me. I love him, and in a few days the divorce will come through. What more do I want? I want peace of mind and trust, and I'll take the blame on myself. Yes — when he comes in, I'll tell him I was wrong, even though I wasn't, and we'll go away tomorrow."
And to keep from thinking any further and being overcome again by irritation, she rang and ordered the trunks brought up so their things could be packed for the country.
At ten o'clock Vronsky came in.

title: Chapter 24
paragraphs: "Well, was it nice?" she asked, coming out to meet him with a meek, apologetic look.

"Just the usual," he answered, seeing at a glance that she was in one of her good moods. He was used to these swings by now, and he was particularly pleased to see it today, as he was in an unusually good mood himself.
"What's this? Now, that's something!" he said, pointing at the boxes in the passage.
"Yes, we have to go. I went out for a drive, and it was so lovely I longed to be in the country. There's nothing keeping you, is there?"
"It's the one thing I want. I'll be right back and we'll talk it over; I only want to change my coat. Order some tea."
And he went into his room.

There was something mortifying in his "Now, that's something" — the way you'd say it to a child who has stopped being naughty — and still more mortifying was the contrast between her contrite tone and his self-confident one. For a moment the urge to fight flared up in her again, but with an effort she beat it down and met Vronsky as good-humoredly as before.
When he came back she told him — partly using sentences she had prepared in advance — how she had spent the day, and her plans for going.

"You know, it came to me almost like an inspiration," she said. "Why wait here for the divorce? Won't it be just the same in the country? I can't wait any longer! I don't want to keep hoping, I don't want to hear another word about the divorce. I've made up my mind it won't have any more bearing on my life. Do you agree?"
"Oh, yes!" he said, glancing uneasily at her keyed-up face.
"What did you do? Who was there?" she asked after a pause.

Vronsky named the guests. "The dinner was first-rate, and so was the boat race, and the whole thing was pleasant enough, but in Moscow they can never do anything without something _ridicule_. A lady of a sort turned up — swimming instructor to the Queen of Sweden — and gave us a demonstration of her skill."
"How? She swam?" Anna asked, frowning.
"In some absurd red _costume de natation;_ and she was old and ugly too. So when are we going?"
"What an absurd thing! Why, did she swim in some special way?" Anna asked, ignoring his question.
"There was absolutely nothing to it. That's just my point — it was awfully stupid. Well then, when do you mean to go?"
Anna shook her head as though trying to shake off an unwelcome thought.
"When? Why, the sooner the better! By tomorrow we won't be ready. The day after."

"Yes... oh, no, wait — the day after tomorrow is Sunday, I have to be at maman's," said Vronsky, awkwardly, because the moment he said his mother's name he felt her staring, suspicious eyes on him. His awkwardness only confirmed her suspicion. She flushed hotly and drew back from him. It wasn't the Queen of Sweden's swimming instructor that filled Anna's imagination now — it was the young Princess Sorokina, who was staying in a village near Moscow with Countess Vronskaya.
"Can't you go tomorrow?" she said.
"Well, no. The deeds and the money I'm going for can't be ready by tomorrow," he answered.
"In that case, we won't go at all."
"But why?"
"I won't go any later. Monday or never!"
"What for?" Vronsky said, as though astonished. "There's no sense in it!"

"There's no sense in it to you, because you don't care about me. You don't care to understand my life. The one thing here I cared about was Hannah. You say it's a pose. Why, yesterday you said I don't love my own daughter, that I love this English girl instead, that it's unnatural. I'd like to know what life would be natural for me!"

For an instant she saw clearly what she was doing, and was horrified at how far she had fallen from her resolve. But even knowing that this was her own ruin, she could not stop herself, could not keep from proving to him that he was in the wrong, could not give in to him.
"I never said that. I said I didn't sympathize with this sudden passion of yours."
"How can you, when you make so much of your straightforwardness, not tell the truth?"
"I never boast and I never tell lies," he said slowly, holding down his rising anger. "It's a great pity if you can't respect...."
"Respect was invented to paper over the empty place where love ought to be. And if you don't love me anymore, it would be better and more honest to say so."

"No, this is becoming unbearable!" Vronsky cried, getting up from his chair. He stopped facing her and said deliberately, "What do you try my patience for?" He looked as though he could have said much more, but was holding himself back. "It has its limits."
"What do you mean by that?" she cried, looking with terror at the open hatred in his whole face, and most of all in his cruel, threatening eyes.
"I was going to say...." he began, then stopped himself. "I have to ask what it is you want from me."

"What can I want? All I can want is that you not leave me, the way you are thinking of doing," she said, understanding everything he had not said. "But I don't really want even that — that's secondary. I want love, and there isn't any. So then everything is over."
She turned toward the door.

"Stop! Sto-op!" said Vronsky, no change in the gloomy lines of his brow, though he caught her by the hand. "What is this all about? I said we have to put off going for three days, and on that you tell me I'm lying, that I'm not an honorable man."

"Yes, and I'll say again that a man who reproaches me for having given up everything for him," she said, dredging up the words of an even earlier quarrel, "is worse than a dishonorable man — he's a heartless one."
"Oh, there are limits to what one can put up with!" he shouted, and dropped her hand.

"He hates me, that's plain," she thought, and without a word or a backward glance she walked unsteadily out of the room. "He loves another woman, that's even plainer," she said to herself as she went into her own room. "I want love, and there isn't any. So then, everything is over." She said again the words she had just spoken: "and it must be ended."
"But how?" she asked herself, and sat down in a low chair before the looking-glass.

Thoughts of where to go now — to the aunt who had brought her up, to Dolly, or simply abroad alone — and of what _he_ was doing now, alone in his study; whether this was the final quarrel or whether reconciliation was still possible; and of what all her old friends in Petersburg would say of her now; and of how Alexey Alexandrovitch would look at it, and a great many other notions about what would come after this rupture — all crowded into her head; but she did not give herself fully to any of them. At the bottom of her heart was some dim idea that alone interested her, and she could not bring it into focus. Thinking again of Alexey Alexandrovitch, she remembered the time of her illness after the birth, and the feeling that had never left her then. "Why didn't I die?" and those words and that feeling came back. And suddenly she knew what was in her soul. Yes — it was the idea that solved everything. "Yes, to die!... And the shame and disgrace for Alexey Alexandrovitch and for Seryozha, and my own dreadful shame — death will save us all from it. To die! And he will be filled with remorse; he'll be sorry; he'll love me; he'll suffer for me." With the trace of a self-pitying smile she sat down in the armchair, taking off and putting on the rings on her left hand, picturing vividly from every angle his feelings after her death.
Approaching footsteps — his footsteps — broke her train of thought. As though absorbed in fitting her rings, she did not even turn toward him.
He came up to her, took her hand, and said softly:
"Anna, we'll go the day after tomorrow if you like. I agree to everything."
She did not answer.
"What is it?" he pressed.
"You know," she said, and at that same instant, unable to hold back any longer, she burst into sobs.

"Throw me out!" she got out between sobs. "I'll go away tomorrow... I'll do more. What am I? An immoral woman! A stone around your neck. I don't want to make you miserable, I don't! I'll set you free. You don't love me — you love somebody else!"
Vronsky begged her to calm down and declared there wasn't the slightest basis for her jealousy; that he had never stopped, and never would stop, loving her; that he loved her more than ever.

"Anna, why torment yourself and me like this?" he said, kissing her hands. There was tenderness in his face now, and she thought she heard tears in his voice and felt them wet on her hand. And in an instant Anna's desperate jealousy turned into a desperate flood of tenderness. She threw her arms around him and covered his head, his neck, his hands with kisses.

title: Chapter 25
paragraphs: Feeling that the reconciliation was complete, Anna threw herself eagerly into preparing for their departure the next morning. Though it was not settled whether they would go on Monday or Tuesday, since each had given way to the other, Anna packed busily, perfectly indifferent now whether they left a day earlier or later. She was standing in her room over an open box, taking things out of it, when he came in to see her earlier than usual, already dressed to go out.
"I'm off straightaway to see maman; she can send me the money through Yegorov. And I'll be ready to leave tomorrow," he said.
Good mood or not, the thought of his visit to his mother's gave her a pang.

"No, I shan't be ready by then myself," she said, and immediately thought: "So it was possible to arrange it the way I wanted, after all." "No, do as you meant to do. Go into the dining room — I'll be along. It's only to sort through these things that aren't wanted," she said, dropping another item onto the heap of finery in Annushka's arms.
Vronsky was eating his beefsteak when she came into the dining room.

"You wouldn't believe how I've come to hate these rooms," she said, sitting down beside him to her coffee. "There's nothing worse than these _chambres garnies_. They have no personality, no soul. These clocks, and curtains, and worst of all the wallpaper — they're a nightmare. I think of Vozdvizhenskoe as the promised land. You're not sending the horses off yet?"
"No, they'll come after us. Where are you going?"
"I was meaning to go to Wilson's to take her some dresses. So it really is tomorrow?" she said brightly; but her face changed all at once.

Vronsky's valet came in to have him sign for a telegram from Petersburg. There was nothing odd in Vronsky's getting a telegram, but he said, as though hiding something from her, that the receipt was in his study, and he turned to her quickly.
"By tomorrow, without fail, I'll have it all wrapped up."
"Who's the telegram from?" she asked, not hearing him.
"From Stiva," he answered reluctantly.
"Why didn't you show it to me? What secret could there be between Stiva and me?"
Vronsky called the valet back and told him to bring the telegram.
"I didn't want to show it to you because Stiva has such a passion for telegraphing — why telegraph when nothing has been settled?"
"About the divorce?"
"Yes; but he says he hasn't managed to get anywhere with it yet. He has promised a definite answer in a day or two. But here it is — read it."
With trembling hands Anna took the telegram and read what Vronsky had told her. At the end was added: "Little hope; but I'll do everything possible and impossible."

"I said yesterday that it's absolutely nothing to me when I get my divorce, or whether I ever get it," she said, flushing scarlet. "There was not the slightest need to hide it from me." "So this is how he can hide, and does hide, his correspondence with women from me," she thought.
"Yashvin meant to come this morning with Voytov," said Vronsky. "I believe he's won everything off Pyevtsov, and more than the man can pay — about sixty thousand."

"No," she said, irritated by his obvious attempt to change the subject, which only showed his own irritation, "why did you suppose this news would hit me so hard that you actually had to hide it? I said I don't want to think about it, and I would have liked you to care as little as I do."
"I care about it because I like things settled," he said.
"What's settled isn't in the form, it's in the love," she said, growing more and more irritated, not by his words but by the tone of cool composure in which he said them. "What do you want it for?"
"My God! Love again," he thought, frowning.
"Oh, you know what for — for your sake and for the children's, in the future."
"There won't be any children in the future."
"That's a great pity," he said.
"You want it for the children's sake, but you don't think of me?" she said, completely forgetting, or never having heard, that he had said, "_For your sake_ and the children's."
The question of whether they could have children had long been a source of dispute and irritation to her. His wanting them she took as proof that he did not value her beauty.
"Oh, I said: for your sake. Above all for your sake," he repeated, frowning as if in pain, "because I'm convinced that most of your irritability comes from the indefiniteness of the position."

"Yes, now he's dropped all pretense, and all his cold hatred for me is in the open," she thought, not catching his words but watching with terror the cold, cruel judge looking mockingly at her out of his eyes.

"That's not the cause," she said, "and, frankly, I don't see how the cause of my irritability, as you call it, can be that I'm entirely in your power. What indefiniteness is there in the position? On the contrary...."
"I'm very sorry that you don't care to understand," he broke in, doggedly intent on getting his point out. "The indefiniteness lies in your imagining that I'm free."
"On that score you can put your mind completely at ease," she said, and turning away from him she began drinking her coffee.

She lifted the cup, her little finger held out apart, and put it to her lips. After a few sips she glanced at him, and from his expression she saw plainly that he was repelled by her hand, by the gesture, by the sound of her lips on the cup.
"I don't care in the least what your mother thinks, or what match she wants to arrange for you," she said, setting down the cup with a shaking hand.
"But we're not talking about that."

"Yes, that's exactly what we're talking about. And let me tell you, a heartless woman, whether she's old or not, whether she's your mother or someone else, is of no consequence to me, and I want nothing to do with her."
"Anna, I beg you not to speak disrespectfully of my mother."
"A woman whose heart can't tell her where her son's happiness and honor lie has no heart."
"I repeat my request that you not speak disrespectfully of my mother, whom I respect," he said, raising his voice and looking at her sternly.

She did not answer. Looking intently at him, at his face, his hands, she went back over every detail of their reconciliation the day before — his passionate caresses. "Just such caresses he has lavished, and will lavish, and longs to lavish on other women!" she thought.
"You don't love your mother. That's all talk, talk, talk!" she said, her eyes full of hatred.
"Even if that were so, you must...."
"Must decide, and I have decided," she said, and she would have walked out, but at that moment Yashvin walked in. Anna greeted him and stayed.

Why, when there was a tempest inside her and she felt herself standing at a turning point in her life that might have terrible consequences — why she had to keep up appearances at that exact moment in front of an outsider who must sooner or later know it all — she could not have said. But damping the storm inside her, she sat down and began talking to their guest.
"Well, how are you getting on? Has your debt been paid?" she asked Yashvin.
"Oh, well enough; I don't suppose I'll get all of it, but I'll get a good half. And when are you off?" said Yashvin, glancing at Vronsky and clearly guessing at a quarrel.
"The day after tomorrow, I think," said Vronsky.
"You've been meaning to go for ages, though."
"But now it's definite," said Anna, looking Vronsky straight in the eye with a look that told him not even to dream of reconciliation.
"Don't you feel sorry for that unlucky Pyevtsov?" she went on, addressing Yashvin.

"I've never asked myself whether I feel sorry for him or not, Anna Arkadyevna. You see, my whole fortune is here" — he tapped his breast pocket — "and just now I'm a wealthy man. But I'm going to the club tonight, and I may come out a beggar. Whoever sits down to play with me wants to leave me without the shirt on my back, and I want the same for him. So we have it out, and that's the fun of it."
"Well, but suppose you were married," said Anna. "How would it be for your wife?"
Yashvin laughed.
"That's why I'm not married, and never mean to be."

"And Helsingfors?" said Vronsky, joining the conversation and glancing at Anna's smiling face. Meeting his eyes, Anna's face went cold and stern in an instant, as though to say to him: "It is not forgotten. Nothing has changed."
"Were you really in love?" she said to Yashvin.

"Oh, heavens — any number of times! But you see, some men can play and yet always lay down their cards when the hour of a _rendezvous_ comes round, while I can take up a love affair so long as it doesn't make me late for my cards in the evening. That's how I manage it."
"No, I didn't mean that — the real thing." She was about to say _Helsingfors_, but wouldn't repeat the word Vronsky had used.
Voytov, who was buying the horse, came in. Anna got up and left the room.

Before leaving the house, Vronsky went into her room. She would have pretended to be looking for something on the table, but ashamed of putting on an act she looked him straight in the face with cold eyes.
"What do you want?" she asked in French.
"To get the guarantee for Gambetta — I've sold him," he said, in a tone that said more clearly than any words: "I haven't time to discuss anything, and it would lead nowhere."

"I'm not to blame in any way," he thought. "If she wants to punish herself, _tant pis pour elle._" But on his way out he thought he heard her say something, and his heart suddenly ached with pity for her.
"Eh, Anna?" he asked.
"I said nothing," she answered, just as coldly and calmly.

"Oh, nothing — _tant pis_ then," he thought, his heart going cold again, and he turned and walked out. As he was going he caught a glimpse in the mirror of her face, white, her lips quivering. He even thought of stopping and saying some word of comfort to her, but his legs carried him out of the room before he could think what to say. He spent the whole day away from home, and when he came in late that night the maid told him that Anna Arkadyevna had a headache and begged him not to come in to her.

title: Chapter 26
paragraphs: Never before had a whole day been spent in a quarrel. Today was the first time. And this was not a quarrel. It was the open acknowledgment of complete coldness. Was it possible to look at her the way he had looked when he came into the room for the guarantee? — to look at her, see her heart breaking with despair, and walk out without a word, with that face of unfeeling calm? He was not merely cold to her, he hated her, because he loved another woman — that was clear.
And recalling all the cruel words he had said, Anna filled in too the words he had plainly wanted to say and might have said to her, and she grew more and more incensed.

"I won't prevent you," he might say. "You can go wherever you like. You were unwilling to be divorced from your husband, no doubt so that you could go back to him. Go back to him. If you want money, I'll give it to you. How many roubles do you want?"
All the cruelest words a brutal man could say, he said to her in her imagination, and she could not forgive him for them, as though he had really said them.
"But didn't he only yesterday swear that he loved me — he, a truthful and sincere man? Haven't I despaired for nothing many times already?" she said to herself afterwards.

All that day, except for her visit to Wilson's, which took up two hours, Anna passed in doubts about whether it was all over or whether there was still hope of reconciliation, whether she should leave at once or see him once more. She waited for him the whole day, and in the evening, going off to her own room and leaving word for him that her head ached, she said to herself, "If he comes in spite of what the maid says, it means he still loves me. If not, it means it's all over, and then I'll decide what to do!..."

In the evening she heard his carriage rumble up to the entrance, his ring, his footsteps, his exchange with the servant; he believed what he was told, didn't ask anything more, and went to his own room. So everything was over.

And death rose up clearly and vividly before her mind as the one means of bringing back love for her in his heart, of punishing him, and of winning the struggle that the evil spirit in possession of her was waging against him.

Now nothing mattered: going to Vozdvizhenskoe or not, getting a divorce from her husband or not — none of it mattered. The one thing that mattered was punishing him. When she poured out her usual dose of opium and thought that she had only to drink off the whole bottle to die, it struck her as so simple and so easy that she began to dwell with pleasure on how he would suffer, repent, and love her memory when it was too late. She lay in bed with open eyes, by the light of a single burned-down candle, gazing at the carved cornice of the ceiling and at the shadow of the screen that fell across part of it, while she pictured to herself in vivid detail how he would feel when she was gone, when she was only a memory to him. "How could I have said such cruel things to her?" he would say. "How could I have left the room without a word to her? But now she's no more. She has gone from us forever. She is...." Suddenly the shadow of the screen wavered, swept across the whole cornice and the whole ceiling; other shadows from the opposite side rushed to meet it; for an instant the shadows flitted back, then with a fresh sweep they leapt forward, wavered, blurred together, and everything went dark. "Death!" she thought. And such horror came over her that for a long time she could not place where she was, and for a long time her trembling hands could not find the matches to light another candle in place of the one that had burned out. "No, anything — only let me live! I love him! He loves me! This has happened before and it will pass," she said, feeling tears of joy at coming back to life trickling down her cheeks. And to escape her panic she hurried to his room.

He was asleep there, and sleeping soundly. She went up to him and held the light above his face and gazed at him a long time. Now, with him asleep, she loved him so much that at the sight of him she could not hold back tears of tenderness. But she knew that if he woke he would look at her with cold eyes, convinced he was in the right, and that before telling him she loved him she would have to prove to him that he had been wrong in his treatment of her. Without waking him she went back, and after a second dose of opium fell, toward morning, into a heavy, broken sleep, in which she never quite lost consciousness.

In the morning she was woken by a horrible nightmare that had recurred several times in her dreams, even before she had taken up with Vronsky. A little old man with an unkempt beard was doing something bent over a piece of iron, muttering meaningless French words, and she, as she always did in this nightmare (which is what made it so dreadful), felt that the peasant was taking no notice of her, but was doing something hideous with the iron — over her. And she woke in a cold sweat.
When she got up, the day before came back to her as though through a mist.

"There was a quarrel. Just what's happened any number of times. I said I had a headache, and he didn't come in to see me. Tomorrow we're going away; I must see him and get ready for the journey," she said to herself. And learning he was in his study, she went down to him. As she passed through the drawing room she heard a carriage stop at the entrance, and looking out of the window she saw the carriage, with a young girl in a lilac hat leaning out, giving directions to the footman as he rang the bell. After some talk in the hall, someone came upstairs, and Vronsky's footsteps could be heard going past the drawing room. He went rapidly down again. Anna looked out of the window once more. She saw him come out onto the steps without his hat and go up to the carriage. The young girl in the lilac hat handed him a parcel. Vronsky, smiling, said something to her. The carriage drove off, and he ran rapidly back upstairs.

The mist that had veiled everything in her soul lifted at once. The feelings of the day before pierced her aching heart with a fresh stab. She could not now understand how she could have lowered herself enough to spend a whole day with him in his house. She went into his room to tell him her decision.

"That was Madame Sorokina and her daughter. They came to bring me the money and the deeds from maman. I couldn't get them yesterday. How's your head — better?" he said calmly, not wanting to see or to take in the dark, set expression on her face.

She looked at him in silence, intently, standing in the middle of the room. He glanced at her, frowned for an instant, then went back to reading a letter. She turned and went deliberately out of the room. He could still have called her back, but she had reached the door and he was still silent, and the only sound was the rustle of the paper as he turned a page.
"Oh, by the way," he said, just as she was at the door, "we're going tomorrow for sure, aren't we?"
"You — but not I," she said, turning back to him.
"Anna, we can't go on like this...."
"You — but not I," she repeated.
"This is becoming unbearable!"
"You... you'll be sorry for this," she said, and walked out.

Alarmed by the desperate look with which she said the words, he jumped up and would have run after her, but on second thought he sat down and scowled, his teeth clenched. This vulgar — as he saw it — threat of something vague infuriated him. "I've tried everything," he thought; "the only thing left is to pay no attention," and he began to get ready to drive into town, and again on to his mother's to get her signature on the deeds.

She heard his footsteps moving about the study and the dining room. At the drawing-room door he stopped. But he didn't come in to her — he simply gave an order that the horse should be handed over to Voytov if he came while he was out. Then she heard the carriage brought round, the door opened, and he stepped out again. But he came back into the porch, and someone went running upstairs. It was the valet, running up for the gloves he had forgotten. She went to the window and saw him take the gloves without looking at them, and, tapping the coachman on the back, say something to him. Then, without glancing up at the window, he settled himself in his usual attitude in the carriage, legs crossed, and pulling on his gloves disappeared round the corner.

title: Chapter 27
paragraphs: "He's gone! It's over!" Anna said to herself, standing at the window; and in answer to this thought the impression of the dark when the candle had gone out, and of her dreadful dream, blended into one and filled her heart with a cold terror.
"No, that can't be!" she cried, and crossing the room she rang the bell. She was so afraid of being alone now that, without waiting for the servant to come in, she went out to meet him.
"Find out where the count has gone," she said. The servant answered that the count had gone to the stables.
"His honor left word that if you cared to drive out, the carriage would be back at once."
"Very good. Wait a moment. I'll write a note right away. Send Mihail with it to the stables. Quickly."
She sat down and wrote:
"I was wrong. Come back home; I must explain. For God's sake come! I'm afraid."
She sealed it and handed it to the servant.
Afraid of being left alone now, she followed the servant out of the room and went to the nursery.

"Why, this isn't it, this isn't him! Where are his blue eyes, his sweet, shy smile?" was her first thought when she saw her chubby, rosy little girl with her black, curly hair, instead of Seryozha, whom in the muddle of her thoughts she had expected to find in the nursery. The little girl, sitting at the table, was stubbornly and noisily banging on it with a cork, staring blankly at her mother with pitch-black eyes. Answering the English nurse that she was quite well, and that she was going to the country the next day, Anna sat down by the little girl and began spinning the cork to amuse her. But the child's loud, ringing laugh and the movement of her eyebrows brought Vronsky back to her so vividly that she got up quickly, holding back her sobs, and went away. "Can it really be all over? No, it can't be!" she thought. "He'll come back. But how will he explain that smile, that animation, after talking to her? But even if he doesn't explain, I'll believe him. If I don't believe him, there's only one thing left for me, and I can't."

She looked at her watch. Twenty minutes had gone by. "By now he's got the note and is on his way back. Not long — ten minutes more.... But what if he doesn't come? No, that can't be. He mustn't see me with tear-stained eyes. I'll go and wash. Yes, yes — did I do my hair or not?" she asked herself. And she couldn't remember. She put her hand to her head. "Yes, my hair has been done, but when I did it I can't possibly recall." She did not trust the evidence of her hand and went up to the pier-glass to see whether she had really done her hair. She had — but she could not remember when. "Who is that?" she thought, looking in the mirror at the swollen face with strangely glittering eyes that stared back at her in fright. "Why, it's me!" she suddenly understood, and looking herself over she seemed to feel his kisses on her, and twitched her shoulders with a shudder. Then she raised her hand to her lips and kissed it.
"What is this? I'm going out of my mind!" and she went into her bedroom, where Annushka was tidying up.
"Annushka," she said, stopping in front of her and staring at the maid, not knowing what to say.
"You were going to see Darya Alexandrovna," the girl said, as though she had understood.
"Darya Alexandrovna? Yes, I'll go."

"Fifteen minutes there, fifteen minutes back. He's coming, he'll be here any moment." She took out her watch and looked at it. "But how could he go off, leaving me in such a state? How can he go on living without making it up with me?" She went to the window and began looking out into the street. By her reckoning he might be back by now. But her counting could be off, and she began again to recall when he had left and to count the minutes.

Just as she had moved over to the big clock to check it against her watch, someone drove up. Glancing out of the window, she saw his carriage. But no one came upstairs, and voices could be heard below. It was the messenger who had come back in the carriage. She went down to him.
"We didn't catch the count. The count had driven off on the lower city road."
"What are you saying? What!..." she said to the rosy, good-humored Mihail as he handed her back the note.
"So he never even got it!" she thought.
"Take this note to Countess Vronskaya's place, you know it? and bring back an answer at once," she said to the messenger.

"And I — what am I going to do?" she thought. "Yes, I'm going to Dolly's, that's right — otherwise I'll go out of my mind. Yes, and I can send a telegram, too." And she wrote a telegram. "I absolutely must talk to you; come at once." After sending the telegram off, she went to dress. When she was dressed and in her hat, she looked again into the eyes of the plump, comfortable-looking Annushka. There was unmistakable sympathy in those good-natured little gray eyes.
"Annushka, dear, what am I to do?" said Anna, sobbing and sinking helplessly into a chair.
"Why fret yourself so, Anna Arkadyevna? There's nothing out of the ordinary in it. You go out for a little drive and it'll cheer you up," said the maid.
"Yes, I'm going," said Anna, pulling herself together and standing up. "And if a telegram comes while I'm out, send it on to Darya Alexandrovna's... no, I'll be back myself."

"Yes, I mustn't think — I must do something, drive somewhere, and above all get out of this house," she said, feeling with terror the strange turmoil going on inside her, and she hurried out to get into the carriage.
"Where to?" asked Pyotr before climbing up onto the box.
"To Znamenka, the Oblonskys'."

title: Chapter 28
paragraphs: The day was bright and sunny. A fine rain had been falling all morning, and it had only just cleared. The iron roofs, the flagstones along the road, the cobbles of the pavement, the wheels and the leather, the brass and the tinplate on the carriages — everything glittered in the May sun. It was three o'clock, the very busiest hour on the streets.

Sitting in a corner of the comfortable carriage that barely swayed on its supple springs, while the grays trotted briskly through the steady rattle of wheels and the shifting impressions in the clean air, Anna ran back over the last few days, and saw her situation in an entirely different light from the one it had worn at home. Now the thought of death no longer struck her as terrible or vivid, and death itself no longer seemed inevitable. Now she reproached herself for the humiliation she had brought herself down to. "I beg him to forgive me. I have given in. I have admitted I was wrong. What for? Can't I live without him?" And without answering the question of how she was going to live without him, she began reading the signs on the shops. "Office and warehouse. Dental surgeon. Yes, I'll tell Dolly the whole thing. She doesn't like Vronsky. I'll be sick and ashamed, but I'll tell her. She loves me, and I'll do what she advises. I won't give in to him; I won't let him train me as he likes. Filippov, bun shop. They say they send their dough all the way to Petersburg. The Moscow water is so good for it. Ah, the springs at Mitishtchen, and the pancakes!"

And she remembered how, very long ago, when she was a girl of seventeen, she had gone with her aunt to Troitsa. "On horseback, too. Was that really me, with those red hands? How much that seemed splendid and out of reach to me then has become worthless, and what I had then is out of my reach for good. Could I ever have believed back then that I would sink to this kind of humiliation? How smug and pleased with himself he'll be when he gets my note! But I'll show him.... How disgusting that paint smells! Why are they always painting and building? _Modes et robes_," she read. A man bowed to her. It was Annushka's husband. "Our parasites," she remembered Vronsky saying. "Our? Why our? The awful thing is that you can't tear the past up by the roots. You can't pull it out, but you can hide your memory of it. And I will hide it." Then she thought of her past with Alexey Alexandrovitch, of how she had erased the memory of it from her life. "Dolly will think I'm leaving my second husband, and so I must surely be in the wrong. As if I cared about being in the right! I can't help it!" she said, and she wanted to cry. But at once she was wondering what those two girls could be smiling about. "Love, probably. They don't know how dreary it is, how cheap.... The boulevard, and the children. Three boys running, pretending to be horses. Seryozha! And I'm losing everything and not getting him back. Yes, I'm losing everything, if he doesn't come back. Maybe he was late for the train and is already back by now. Wanting to be humiliated again!" she said to herself. "No, I'll go to Dolly, and tell her straight out, I'm unhappy, I deserve this, I'm to blame, but I'm still unhappy, help me. These horses, this carriage — how loathsome I am to myself in this carriage — it's all his; but I won't be looking at any of it again."
Turning over the words she would use with Dolly, and deliberately working her heart up into a bitter pitch, Anna went upstairs.
"Is someone with her?" she asked in the hall.
"Katerina Alexandrovna Levin," answered the footman.

"Kitty! Kitty, the one Vronsky was in love with!" Anna thought. "The girl he thinks about with love. He regrets not marrying her. Me he thinks about with hatred, and regrets ever having had anything to do with me."
The sisters were in the middle of a conversation about nursing when Anna arrived. Dolly came down alone to see the visitor who had interrupted them.
"So you haven't left yet? I meant to come over to you," she said. "I had a letter from Stiva today."
"We had a telegram too," Anna answered, looking around for Kitty.
"He writes that he can't quite work out what Alexey Alexandrovitch wants, but he won't leave without a definite answer."
"I thought you had someone with you. Can I see the letter?"
"Yes — Kitty," Dolly said, embarrassed. "She stayed in the nursery. She has been very ill."
"So I heard. May I see the letter?"
"I'll get it right now. But he isn't refusing; in fact, Stiva has hopes," Dolly said, pausing in the doorway.
"I don't have any, and honestly I don't want any," said Anna.

"What's this? Does Kitty think it's beneath her to meet me?" Anna thought, alone now. "Maybe she's right. But it's not for her, the girl who was in love with Vronsky — it's not for her to make me feel it, even if it's true. I know that in my position no decent woman can receive me. I knew that from the first moment I sacrificed everything for him. And this is my reward! Oh, how I hate him! And what did I come here for? I feel worse here, more wretched." She could hear the sisters consulting in the next room. "And what am I going to say to Dolly now? Amuse Kitty with the sight of my misery, put up with her condescension? No; besides, Dolly wouldn't understand. There's no point in telling her. The only interesting thing would be to see Kitty, and show her how I despise everyone and everything, how nothing matters to me anymore."
Dolly came back with the letter. Anna read it and handed it back without a word.
"I knew all of that already," she said, "and it doesn't interest me in the least."
"Oh, why not? On the contrary, I have hopes," Dolly said, looking at Anna with curious attention. She had never seen her this strangely on edge. "When are you leaving?" she asked.
Anna, half-closing her eyes, stared straight ahead and did not answer.
"Why does Kitty avoid me?" she said, looking at the door and flushing red.

"Oh, that's nonsense! She's nursing, and it isn't going right, and I've been giving her advice.... She's pleased you're here. She'll be down in a minute," Dolly said awkwardly, never any good at lying. "There — here she is."
When she had heard that Anna was downstairs, Kitty had wanted to stay away, but Dolly had talked her into it. Pulling herself together, Kitty came in, walked up to Anna, blushing, and shook her hand.
"I'm so glad to see you," she said in an unsteady voice.

Kitty had been thrown off by the inner struggle between her hostility toward this bad woman and her wish to be kind to her. But the moment she saw Anna's lovely, attractive face, all hostility vanished.
"I wouldn't have been surprised if you hadn't wanted to see me. I'm used to everything by now. You've been ill? Yes, you've changed," said Anna.

Kitty sensed that Anna was looking at her with hostility. She put this hostility down to the awkward position Anna, who had once condescended to her, must feel with her now, and she felt sorry for her.
They talked about Kitty's illness, about the baby, about Stiva, but it was obvious that none of it interested Anna.
"I came to say good-bye," she said, getting up.
"Oh, when are you leaving?"
But again without answering, Anna turned to Kitty.

"Yes, I'm very glad I got to see you," she said with a smile. "I've heard so much about you from everyone, even from your husband. He came to see me, and I liked him enormously," she said, unmistakably meaning harm by it. "Where is he?"
"He has gone back to the country," Kitty said, blushing.
"Give him my regards, make sure you do."
"I will, definitely!" Kitty said naively, looking at her with compassion in her eyes.
"So good-bye, Dolly." And kissing Dolly and shaking Kitty's hand, Anna went out in a hurry.
"She's exactly the same, and just as charming! She's so lovely!" Kitty said, once she was alone with her sister. "But there's something pitiful about her. Terribly pitiful!"
"Yes, there's something unusual about her today," Dolly said. "When I walked her into the hall, I had the feeling she was almost crying."

title: Chapter 29
paragraphs: Anna climbed back into the carriage in an even worse state than when she had set out from home. On top of everything else she had already been suffering, there was now the sense of degradation and exclusion she had felt so sharply in front of Kitty.
"Where to? Home?" Pyotr asked.
"Yes, home," she said, no longer really paying attention to where she was going.

"The way they looked at me, as though I were something dreadful, baffling, fascinating! What can he be saying to the other one with such enthusiasm?" she thought, staring at two men walking past. "Can anyone ever really tell anyone else what they feel? I meant to tell Dolly, and it's a good thing I didn't. She would have been thrilled at my misery! She would have hidden it, but underneath she would have been glad I was being punished for the happiness she envied me. Kitty would have been even more pleased. I can see right through her! She knows I was unusually nice to her husband. And she's jealous, and she hates me. And she despises me. In her eyes I'm an immoral woman. If I were an immoral woman, I could have made her husband fall in love with me ... if I'd wanted to. And, in fact, I did want to. There's someone who's pleased with himself," she thought, watching a fat, ruddy gentleman come toward her. He took her for an acquaintance and lifted his shiny hat over his bald, shiny head, then realized his mistake. "He thought he knew me. Well, he knows me as well as anyone in the world does. I don't know myself. I know my appetites, as the French put it. Those boys want that dirty ice cream — that they know for certain," she thought, looking at two boys who had stopped an ice cream seller, who had taken the barrel off his head and was wiping his sweating face with a towel. "We all want something sweet and nice. If not candy, then a filthy ice. And Kitty's the same — if not Vronsky, then Levin. And she envies me and hates me. And we all hate each other. I hate Kitty, Kitty hates me. Yes, that's the truth. '_Tiutkin, coiffeur._' _Je me fais coiffer par Tiutkin...._ I'll tell him that when he comes home," she thought, and smiled. But the same instant she remembered that there was no longer anyone she could tell something amusing to. "And there's nothing amusing, nothing to laugh about, really. It's all hateful. They're singing vespers, and look how carefully that merchant is crossing himself — as if he were afraid of missing a beat. Why all these churches and all this singing and all this humbug? Just to disguise the fact that we all hate each other, like those cab drivers yelling at each other so viciously. Yashvin says, 'He wants to strip me of my shirt, and I want to strip him of his.' Yes, that's the truth!"

She was so absorbed in these thoughts that she stopped thinking about her own situation, and the carriage drew up at the steps of her house. It was only when she saw the porter hurrying out to meet her that she remembered she had sent the note and the telegram.
"Any answer?" she asked.
"I'll check right now," the porter answered, and glancing into his lodge, he took out and handed her the thin square envelope of a telegram. "Cannot come before ten. — Vronsky," she read.
"And the messenger hasn't come back?"
"No," the porter answered.

"Then, that being so, I know what I have to do," she said, and with a vague fury and craving for revenge rising up in her, she ran up the stairs. "I'll go to him myself. Before I leave forever, I'll tell him everything. I have never hated anyone the way I hate that man!" she thought. Seeing his hat on the rack, she shuddered with disgust. She wasn't taking in the fact that his telegram was a reply to her telegram and that he had not yet received her note. She pictured him calmly chatting with his mother and Princess Sorokina and gloating over her suffering. "Yes, I have to go right away," she said, without yet knowing where she was going. She longed to get out as quickly as possible from the feelings she had just lived through in that hideous house. The servants, the walls, the things in that house — everything filled her with revulsion and hatred and pressed down on her like a weight.

"Yes, I have to go to the railway station, and if he isn't there, then go on out there and catch him." Anna looked up the railway timetable in the newspapers. An evening train left at two minutes past eight. "Yes, I'll make it." She gave orders for the fresh horses to be put to, and packed a few days' worth of necessities into a traveling bag. She knew she would never come back here again.

Among the plans running through her head she vaguely settled on this: after whatever happened at the station or at the countess's house, she would go on as far as the first town on the Nizhni line and stop there.

Dinner was on the table; she went down, but the smell of the bread and cheese was enough to make every kind of food disgust her. She ordered the carriage and went out. The house cast a shadow now all the way across the street, but it was a bright evening and the sun was still warm. Annushka, coming down with her things, and Pyotr, loading them into the carriage, and the coachman, who was clearly in a bad mood, were all hateful to her, and grated on her with everything they said and did.
"I don't need you, Pyotr."
"What about the ticket, then?"
"Well, as you like, it doesn't matter," she snapped.
Pyotr jumped onto the box, planted his hands on his hips, and told the coachman to drive to the booking office.
